entry.title: Presence Is Enough [Memos]
entry.content:
From when I was very small until I finished college, I always wished my dad would stay home a few more days over Spring Festival.

Truth is, even when he was home he didn't spend all his time with us. He'd go out to play cards during the day and go out drinking at night, so the time we spent together was mostly at mealtimes and before bed.

Even so, the feeling of him being there was completely different.

After I started working, I became the first one to leave home after Spring Festival.

Later, when I went home, I'd sometimes just sit on the sofa reading or playing on my phone. My sister would ask why I didn't get out more and talk to people, and I'd answer with what I've always thought: every year I come home and just sit here without saying a word, and that alone makes everything different.

Looking back now, much of the time it really is a comfort just to have the people who matter there. Everything else is secondary.

entry.title: Energy Is the Precondition for Living Well
entry.content:
Three Days of Qingming

The day before the Qingming holiday (a Chinese spring festival for tending ancestors' graves), I went to bed half an hour early. On the first morning of the holiday I was bursting with energy and raring to go, and even dashed off a blog post, A Wrong Map Is Better Than No Map.

I thought, if half an hour early makes this much difference, imagine what happens if I go to bed even earlier. I'll take off.
So that day I tried sleeping at nine. I woke up at three in the morning and could not for the life of me fall back asleep, scrolled my phone for half an hour, and then managed to sleep through to seven.

I figured that with all that sleep I'd be full of energy yesterday. Instead, after breakfast and a coffee, I sat down at my desk and started nodding off, yawning nonstop. I flipped through a few ebooks and felt like I couldn't catch my breath, then picked up a paper book on alternative data and found it dull too.

So I stopped pretending and went back to sleep a little after ten in the morning, drifting in and out until noon. I got up, had lunch, and thought, surely I've slept enough now; I'll grab a coffee and grind straight through to dinner. But I was in the same state as in the morning, couldn't even hold a book, and before three I couldn't hold out any longer. I even had a bit of a physical headache. Damn it. Back to fucking sleep.

I drifted along until after five, then biked out for some Henan food. Riding past the bustling Big Roof, I finally felt a little bit alive again.
I was still sleepy in the evening, but to get back to a normal rhythm I forced myself to stay up until eleven, then slept straight through to seven-thirty.

When I woke up this morning, that muddled feeling from yesterday was finally gone. I was raring to go again and spent a very productive morning reading.

Comparing these three days, I really felt how important it is to look after your energy. Being driven and clear-headed versus being drowsy and worn out, with your head under a slow fog: those are two completely different people.
Yesterday I even started to suspect I'd gone lazy again, that Lu Shen's influence had worn off, and for a while I felt a real fear of backsliding. But comparing it with today, I'm sure it was only an energy problem, not a willingness problem.

Your body clock is hard to break casually. Right now the sleep window that suits me best is from eleven at night to seven-thirty in the morning. Minus the time it takes to fall asleep, that's just about eight hours. Once I drift outside that window, even drinking coffee like water doesn't do shit.

Lazy men and lazy women may just be products of low energy

Lazy men and lazy women are probably the most off-putting creatures in this world. Even when you want to help them, it feels like trying to prop up a pile of mud against the wall.

I'm not naturally a very energetic person. According to my BaZi (Chinese birth-chart astrology), I'm short on Fire among the five elements, so my spirit tends to turn inward.
In my own experience this actually matched up, and so it quietly became a self-fulfilling prophecy. In the past I often felt low on energy and assumed it was just my constitution. But comparing different ways of living over the past few years has convinced me that's really not the case. Without the comparison, you simply can't tell what a good state of living feels like.

Enough sleep at the right time (7 to 8 hours) + consistent exercise (for me, biking to and from work when it isn't raining, 25 km round trip): keep it up for half a year and your cardiovascular fitness and energy go up a level. As long as you don't break the routine on a whim, most days you'll have plenty of energy.

The old habits of only wanting to lie down on holidays, not being able to sit still at my desk, and not bothering with housework, all more or less learned helplessness, have completely disappeared, and I've come to experience the steady, always-improving way of living that Lu Shen has.
So much so that these days I really can't stand the lazy-man, lazy-woman state, including but not limited to:

  1. Staying up late at night, numbly scrolling your phone and binge-watching shows
  2. Lazing around in the morning and not being able to get out of bed
  3. Being listless all day, never sitting when you could lie down
  4. Doing housework sloppily, for example washing the dishes but not cleaning the sink, leaving paper towels everywhere, closing the window but not the screen, always doing only 80%. This matters especially for keeping a clean and tidy home: let that remaining 20% pile up for three days and the place becomes a nightmare.
  5. Reading, studying and working in fits and starts: fishing for three days, drying the nets for two
  6. ...

But all of these problems can be fixed bit by bit as long as you stay energetic.
And to stay energetic, a certain amount of self-discipline is indispensable. Especially for people who lack a sense of meaning and mission, it may even take some external constraint to complete the "enlightenment" process.

And once someone has experienced the contrast between the two states, I don't think anyone would fail to prefer a tidier, fuller life.

entry.title: A Wrong Map Is Better Than No Map
entry.content:
I got up too early yesterday, and with a team lunch eating into my midday nap, I went to bed before ten.

A quarter of 2024 is already gone. A night of rain has added a little more melancholy to the Qingming festival (the day Chinese families tend their ancestors' graves), but I'm in Hangzhou and can't go home to put fresh earth on the old graves of my forebears. After breakfast I made a cup of coffee and sat down by the window to sort through what I've been thinking and feeling lately.

My biggest cumulative gain of the whole first quarter was finishing Scholar's Advanced Technological System (a Chinese web novel), a hardcore science-fiction novel let down by its title. The author's academic range and prose are both solid. The main thread follows Lu Zhou, an academic prodigy, through his explorations in mathematics, as he pushes physics, biochemistry, materials science, energy, information science and human civilization as a whole forward.

Some people say a few of the book's details are quite wrong. Others say that even they, as outsiders, can tell the author is fooling outsiders.

To me, the first is a normal criticism. The second is just short-sightedness; that reader might as well not have read the book.

For me, the book pushed further the process of connecting the dots between some key experiences from my past, and it gave me a framework-level understanding of the central disciplines of today's world and their central questions. That is exactly why I called it a "cumulative gain" above: accumulation presupposes some consistent main thread. For me the big thread is how far I have come in experiencing and understanding the natural world and human society. The more focused sub-threads are investing and computing. But as I said in About me, understanding the world is the bigger question, the foundation of all foundations.

Which dots got connected?

The ACM campus contest, Ah Huang's transcendental number, USTC's admissions exam, a primary-school contest

When I took part in the campus round of the ACM programming contest in college, one problem involved very large numbers, that is, numbers beyond what 32-bit or 64-bit binary can represent. You need something like the built-in long long type some languages provide. Whether a language has built-in big-number handling isn't really the point. The point is that I had no background knowledge about big numbers at all, so I designed the algorithm with ordinary integer and floating-point types. Naturally the precision wasn't enough and the results were way off.

Only later did I learn that this is "the problem of limited precision in how computers and the C language represent data". My first reaction on learning it was: "What the hell, our college C course never taught this. Isn't this problem beyond the syllabus?"

Once in high school I ran into a hard math problem and felt I had cobbled together an answer. When I discussed it with Ah Huang, a classmate sitting next to me, he glanced at my result and said: your answer is wrong, because the problem is about a polynomial with integer coefficients, and your answer has a transcendental number in it. Me: ?????

Before that, I went from my county town to Zhengzhou to sit the independent admissions exam of USTC (the University of Science and Technology of China). Almost every question on the paper involved knowledge I had never seen. Beyond the syllabus, absolutely beyond the syllabus, damn it.

An even earlier memory: in first grade I entered a competition and did terribly. Later I heard that only second or third graders, or even third and fourth graders, could have had the knowledge it required.

A flash of insight: the valley of death on the learning curve, and the point of enlightenment

At first I assumed situations like these were much the same for everyone my age: some knew a bit more, some a bit less, but no qualitative difference.
So I never dug into it, and unfortunately no one was around to point it out to me. Only after several years of work, meeting more people and seeing more things, did my horizons widen enough for me to gradually understand what it meant.

1/ The point of enlightenment in learning.
On the learning path of every skill or discipline there is a critical point on the climb, which I call a true point of enlightenment, in exactly the sense Kant meant in his essay "What Is Enlightenment?".1
Past this point, the student has walked out of the valley of death and can use their own reason to explore the much larger map still covered in fog.
Fail to get past it, and once the guidance stops, they keep circling and repeating at a low level, or even slide backwards.

2/ How to tell whether someone has reached it.
My own test is whether the student has built a small framework map out of what they already know, whether they have a vague picture of where things go from here, and whether, when they meet a suitable piece of knowledge, they can judge without anyone's help whether it fits into the map they already have and connects to it.

Only then has the master truly "led them through the door" (as the Chinese saying goes, the master leads you through the door, and the practice is up to you).

Only then do they have the foundation for taking in a high-volume flow of information.

3/ High-volume information input.
From what I later learned about the admissions results, plenty of people could indeed handle the questions that were beyond my syllabus. That was when I realized what "real teaching resources" mean, and what "material prepared for students with capacity to spare" means. The horizons of big-city teaching teams and the learning resources available there are simply not something a small county town can match, and they produced a cohort of talented students with very wide horizons. The questions that were beyond our syllabus had long been within their view. The shock I felt when Ah Huang mentioned transcendental numbers made me feel the gap deeply, and later I found many students like Ah Huang among my college classmates.

When I was at Liulou Primary School, my family didn't own a single book outside the textbooks. I coveted the school's little library room, but it was never opened to students before I graduated. In fourth grade I worked up the courage to ask the headmaster if I could borrow a book. He said all he had was Marx's Capital. I said Capital would do. He said even he couldn't understand that book, and didn't take me seriously. In the end I never borrowed a single book.
Going to middle school in the county town was painful but the right thing. With money I saved I bought Sherlock Holmes and Science Fiction World (a Chinese science-fiction magazine), and was lucky enough to pick up some popular-science magazines at a stall selling miscellaneous books. Sherlock Holmes and Science Fiction World in particular still have a very visible influence on me today.
Of course, back then nobody sold advanced reading for the main academic track. The only advanced book I read in high school was Chen Yuezeng's General Biology, borrowed from Ah Huang, and it influenced me a lot too.

Come to think of it, it makes sense. Having never been exposed to any of that, how could I possibly answer those questions by transferring knowledge?
When the difficulty in front of you lies too far beyond your knowledge and horizons, the gap is hard to cross. Besides, some knowledge simply cannot be derived from more basic knowledge. You can't work out integration on the spot in an exam hall from basic arithmetic.

4/ Drop the idea of "beyond the syllabus" entirely.
Perhaps this is what competitions are for. They tell contestants that there is no syllabus in any absolute sense in this world, and therefore no such thing as "beyond the syllabus". They demand that contestants broaden their horizons, recognize that a bigger picture exists, accumulate, lift the fog covering the areas humanity has already explored bit by bit, and then explore the edges of the picture.

For people with plenty of life experience this is easier to grasp. No one is going to draw a boundary around the problems you face in real life and promise you'll find the answer as long as you search inside it.

And to let go of this idea and look for solutions across a wider range, building a vague but global framework matters most of all.

Columbus and the maps of the Age of Discovery

Before the Age of Discovery, European maps mixed science, speculation and theology. They covered only the known world of Europe, parts of Asia and the northern coast of Africa, and their accuracy varied enormously. Take, for example, the world map drawn in the late 15th century by the cartographer Henricus Martellus Germanus 2:

Columbus, a navigator of the same late 15th century, relied early on precisely these error-ridden maps. The Age of Discovery he went on to open fundamentally changed mapmaking: as explorers returned from new lands, cartographers folded the new information into their maps, vastly extending the reach of world maps and improving their accuracy.

In hindsight, those early maps, full of holes as they were, gave people a macro framework of the world and a precious sense of finiteness. That finiteness and framework gave the courageous pioneers more confidence to explore the whole world and to look for new sea routes, and that exploration would in turn correct the errors and make both the framework and the details more precise.

A map full of errors is far better than no map at all

If you can meet or find a teacher, textbook, novel, article or any other means that suits you and gives you a top-down framework map, please don't miss it, and certainly don't give up such a precious opportunity just because someone says it has a few small mistakes.

  1. Kant's essay is well worth reading. A Chinese translation is available at: http://www.personpsy.org/uploadfiles/file/opentheeyes/culture/2020/什么是启蒙康德.pdf ↩
  2. See the Wikipedia entry: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henricus_Martellus_Germanus ↩

entry.title: A Short History of the Web: The Key Threads
entry.content:
Over the past two or three years I have learned a lot from the history of the Web. It also fits the way I like to learn complex systems: understand the old paradigm and how it developed, then move on to the new paradigm and the problems at the frontier.

The Web's original paradigm metaphor: it started as "a hypertext application"

1980: Tim Berners-Lee and ENQUIRE

From June to December 1980, Tim Berners-Lee worked as an independent contractor at the vast CERN 1.

While there, he learned that CERN had roughly 10,000 staff, each with different hardware, software and personal requirements, and that much of the work got done through email and file exchange.

He clearly saw a Tech Space here, that is, room to use technology to help researchers share and update information with one another. So he built a new hypertext prototype system called ENQUIRE2.

Looking at it from today's vantage point:

  1. This prototype was really a simple, app-level hypertext program, something like today's Wikipedia, or note-taking systems such as Notion, Flomo and Obsidian.
  2. Any software designed at the app level is similar: the system defines too much around its particular use case and requires users to organize their content according to its rules, which means its extensibility is bound to be limited.
  3. What the real Web needed was something that connects and organizes all these app-level things, Wikipedia, Notion, Flomo, Feishu, Google Docs, Obsidian and so on, at a higher level.

Clearly, only a higher degree of abstraction could deliver that more general capability.

1989: A higher abstraction

After leaving CERN at the end of 1980, Tim Berners-Lee spent three years in business related to computer networking (at the time the bottom layer of networks was TCP/IP, with various application-layer protocols such as FTP on top). As someone with deep technical understanding and real insight into how a business runs, and working on a real-time remote procedure call project at that, he evidently absorbed a great deal of network design thinking from that experience. In 1984 he returned to CERN.

More experience, and his years of work on computer networks, made him realize that hoping to unify CERN's documentation through one app-level tool was unrealistic. He needed some way to link different documentation systems (many of them coexisted at CERN, including his own ENQUIRE):

Creating the web was really an act of desperation, because the situation without it was very difficult when I was working at CERN later.
Most of the technology involved in the web, like the hypertext, like the Internet, multifont text objects, had all been designed already.
I just had to put them together. It was a step of generalizing, going to a higher level of abstraction, thinking about all the documentation systems out there as being possibly part of a larger imaginary documentation system.
But then the engineering was fairly straightforward. It was designed in order to make it possible to get at documentation and in order to be able to get people — students working with me, contributing to the project, for example — to be able to come in and link in their ideas, so that we wouldn't lose it all if we didn't debrief them before they left.
Really, it was designed to be a collaborative workspace for people to design on a system together. That was the exciting thing about it.

—— Academy of Achievement interview with Tim Berners-Lee, 2007: Visionary of the Internet 3

(By "the situation without it" he means the pain of working across many documentation systems at once. "The Internet" here is the underlying internet, which is not the same thing as the World Wide Web.)

Based on these ideas, he designed and submitted the Web proposal 4, shown below:

He also built humanity's first web browser, the first web server, and a prototype website, http://info.cern.ch 5

The earliest prototype contained three core technologies, and you can tell from the names alone that they were born to "link different hypertext systems":

  1. HTML: HyperText Markup Language.
    The markup (formatting) language for the web.

  2. URI: Uniform Resource Identifier.
    A kind of "address" that is unique and used to identify to each resource on the web. It is also commonly called a URL.

  3. HTTP: Hypertext Transfer Protocol.
    Allows for the retrieval of linked resources from across the web.

Again, looking at it from today:

  1. These three elements are highly abstract. By following a few simple conventions, a user can run a documentation system entirely under their own control (rather than writing their documents inside a software structure someone else controls), or adapt an existing documentation system so that it can link to others. This forms the basic framework of the modern Web.
  2. The first browser was already a container space that could hold many different websites.
  3. The primary motivation at this point was linking different documentation systems. Unlike the operating systems of the day, it was not driven by heavier business-workflow needs, so naturally there was no CSS or JavaScript, which only came later.

All in all, the Web's basic architecture was settled from the very first version.
A highly abstract mechanism at the application layer (still far more concrete, of course, than lower-level abstractions like TCP/IP), plus a natural, distributed openness, formed an enormous space for collaboration.

Tim Berners-Lee's original top-down design had achieved its goal. What remained were larger forces of the era: the growth of personal computers, the businesses built on them, networks becoming a high-speed information medium for human activity, and so on. These began to drive the Web's development in the other direction, from the bottom up.

1991 – 2007: Three browsers, Mosaic, Netscape and IE

This was the early era of browsers. Its landmark events include:

  1. 1993: CGI
    The National Center for Supercomputing Applications (NCSA) released the NCSA HTTPd web server, which included an early version of CGI. This allowed server-side web programs to run in response to page requests, marking the birth of dynamic content on the web. Dynamic content was quite limited back then, of course: submitting a form, that kind of thing.

  2. 1994: CSS is invented
    CSS was first proposed by Håkon Wium Lie on October 10, 1994. In 1996 the W3C endorsed it as the CSS1 Recommendation. Its original goal was better typographic control over documents, mainly document layout; it didn't even have a well-defined "frame layout" mechanism.

  3. 1995: JavaScript
    In 1995, Brendan Eich, working at Netscape, invented JavaScript, and it shipped in version 2.0 of the Netscape browser. There was clearly a business need here too, and as a new technical feature it helped Netscape's browser stay ahead.

Back to our present-day view again:

  1. In this phase, the context of the time and concrete needs limited people's imagination. Many designs were driven bottom-up by business needs, with little forward-looking design.
  2. CSS was originally aimed mostly at document typesetting (the way Word does it). It struggled when used for two-dimensional page layout, and many capabilities that are routine in graphic design had to be achieved by hacking a one-dimensional flow layout.
  3. JavaScript was originally meant for small tasks inside web pages; it was not a carefully thought-out language. Fortunately, the requirements for a universal Turing machine are simple, and JavaScript is Turing complete too (it has sequential execution, conditional branching and loops). Given enough APIs, it can in theory do anything any other language can.
  4. Because the Web is open, as the system grew, web developers and browser makers had to stay compatible with and accommodate one another. Every web developer wants their pages to render correctly in browsers, and every browser wants to render every page. Together this created strong path dependence on technologies already implemented: anything new had to be compatible with what already existed. That guaranteed openness and usability, but it also piled up a large historical debt for the Web.
  5. Standards bodies with real authority began to emerge. The W3C, led by Tim Berners-Lee, has led the HTML and CSS specifications all along, and the venerable ECMA took over standardizing JavaScript6.

Personally, I think these three browsers and the new technologies they introduced all belong to one paradigm of thought: they kept moving forward along the path of Tim Berners-Lee's browser prototype.

In this period users had limited interaction with content; web pages were purely informational and static. But that was bound to be a short-lived phase.

Because the Web is public and easy to access, humanity had for the first time a shared information medium, a tool no earlier era ever had. Demand was simply enormous. Quantitative change, piling up, brings qualitative change: bottom-up demand kept pushing Web technology forward and placed ever higher demands on the engineering design of the Web as a whole.

Once people no longer wanted websites to be simple text pages but complete apps that could carry all kinds of business logic, what they wanted from the browser also shifted, from a single tool for displaying pages to an all-purpose, OS-like platform.

The Web's paradigm shift: from "a hypertext application" to "an operating system platform"

From here on, we're back to things most of us know well.

2000 – 2010: The rise of Amazon's cloud services

This too is background from the era. The main story of this period was remote computer clusters and operating-system virtualization. The rapid growth of server-side capability laid the foundation for thin clients.

2008: The V8 engine

Chrome's V8 JavaScript engine7 greatly improved JavaScript's runtime capability and efficiency.

2009: ChromeOS

Google announced the project in July 2009, initially describing it as a cloud-first operating system in which applications and user data would live in the cloud. ChromeOS was mainly for running web applications.

2005 onward: The CSS3 standard

Work on CSS3 began as early as 2005.
It aimed to meet the need for more dynamic and interactive web design and layouts that adapt to all kinds of devices (responsive design), screens and user interactions. Concretely, this includes media queries, the Flexbox model, Grid layout, and richer animation.
On the engineering side, it also brought modularity into the CSS specification, allowing features to be developed and adopted independently.

In short: stronger layout and interaction across different devices, and a more engineering-oriented design, to cope with increasingly complex needs.

2015: ECMAScript 6

Discussion of the next version began almost immediately after ES5 was released in 2009, and the ES6 standard was officially released in 2015.
ES6's biggest improvements were native support for modules, more convenient asynchronous calls, improved variable scoping, and a more object-oriented Class syntactic sugar.

2015: PWA

Alex Russell and Frances Berriman of Google coined the term "Progressive Web App" to describe applications that take advantage of new features supported by modern browsers, including service workers, manifests and other web platform features.

2018: Apple starts supporting PWAs

Of course, PWAs conflict with Apple's business ecosystem, and Apple's support for them is incomplete.

Likewise, looking at it from today:

  1. The most fundamental paradigm became "treat the browser the way you treat an operating system." With that as the backdrop, the overall direction of engineering became very clear.
  2. Standards actually lag behind real needs. Before new standards like CSS3 and ES6 were written, there were already countless similar engineering practices: all sorts of hacky layout techniques in CSS; module conventions like CommonJS and AMD in JavaScript; jQuery's wrapper around document selectors; and so on. CSS3 and ES6 borrowed heavily from and absorbed these practices. You could say these standards were the result of the whole Web community pushing.
  3. Beyond the community push, a Web designed around the "operating system metaphor" could borrow more and more from OS app programming and absorb the more carefully considered language designs of Java, Python and others.

In short, as the underlying tech stack and engineering architecture matured, the Web became an operating system platform in the true sense. Web applications matured too, and came closer and closer to the experience of native apps.

Some discussion from a WeChat group

The Web is the most far-reaching revolutionary technology of the information age (probably no need to say "one of the most"), and its inventor, Tim Berners-Lee, is still alive. His views on the Web are well worth following.

This post was originally prompted by a Web-related discussion in a WeChat group. Newcomers to the field always seem to have similar confusions (and this friend is fairly sensitive to certain phenomena).

entry.title: Reopening My Independent Blog
entry.content:
Maybe it's just like that famous curve, from the Peak of Mount Stupid down into the Valley of Despair and up the Slope of Enlightenment: life is one cycle of tinkering after another.

The Past

In the first post on this blog, Origins, I quoted someone else's summary of the three stages of blogging:

Stage one: you've just discovered blogging, it feels fresh, and you try writing on some free hosting service.
Stage two: you find the free service too restrictive, so you buy your own domain and hosting and set up an independent blog.
Stage three: you find managing an independent blog too much hassle, and ideally you'd keep control while someone else handles the management, so you only have to write.

But after planting that flag, I only wrote on my independent blog for a year. When it came time to renew the domain, keeping my own domain going felt like a chore, so I gave the blog up.
After that I moved through Zhihu (a Chinese Q&A site), WeChat Official Accounts, and Xiaobaotong (a Chinese paid-newsletter platform) as places to publish my writing. I had thought that, just like the three stages above, handing my writing over to these platforms would let me focus more on the essence of writing. In practice, it was the exact opposite.

What Brought Me Back

Looking back, a few things led me to return to an independent blog.

1. These platforms are not convenient to use
Want to publish something publicly on them?
First you have to log in, then click around to find the publishing center, and only then can you write your first line (the editors on Zhihu and WeChat in particular are beyond words).

2. Playing away from home, without freedom
Almost every platform has its own explicit or implicit rules: what you can and can't write, what spreads easily, what sinks without a trace. These unspoken things shape my choice of topics and make me anxious.

All things considered, almost no writing platform is actually as convenient to write on as an independent blog. An independent blog does need some maintenance, but on the whole it's fairly infrequent. And more importantly, it gives you freedom.

3. I have engineering skills
After I left ByteDance in 2020, maybe because I came into contact with new things, maybe because I let go of some old obsessions, or maybe because I ran into a lot of problems in those years, with relationships and with my family's health, after a few years of struggle my view suddenly widened a great deal. I saw my own limits clearly, and society's limits, and I also saw what choices I should make within those constraints to keep going and keep living.

I also truly began to realize that technology is a very effective lever and a form of productivity, something that lets you make real changes by creating things.
Creating matters. Writing an article is creating, and using your own skills to build an independent product is creating too, and the latter compounds more strongly.

4. Some people's influence
Liu Shaonan, Bai Guang, and the indie developers on Jike (a Chinese social app) passionately searching for their own small business.
Huang Yan and Jiuzhang, whose independent blogs are still alive and still being updated.

Spending time around these people, I could feel the courage it takes to explore independence while being swept along by this huge, chaotic, noisy current of the world.

All in all, I've started to want to create things with a longer life span, and over these years I happen to have learned the skills to do it. Just as settling down in Hangzhou after turning thirty ended more than a decade of feeling adrift, these past two years I've increasingly wanted a home ground of my own, with all my writing gathered in one place.

What Changed

While trying to restore the old blog, I realized how carelessly I used to treat my writing. When I left ByteDance and switched computers, I backed up a lot of material, but not the source files of the old blog. Luckily, the GitHub repository still had the compiled files, so I restored the posts one by one, and one by one I reread those old articles from 2016. The writing is very immature, sometimes even deliberately mystifying, yet to me it somehow felt new every time I read it.

While rereading, I also found that many of the external links were dead. Some pointed to other people's independent blogs, some to general websites, and some even to ByteDance's old CDN image host. The GitHub and Google links, however, all still work.

Eight years really is a long time. Many things have changed or simply no longer exist, and some haven't changed at all. Putting them side by side makes you sigh.

Besides restoring the old stuff, there are a few changes:

  • The blog's name changed from "Xiaohu Ruwei" (The Little Fox Wets Its Tail, an image from the I Ching) to the more concrete "Knots & Nets"
  • I designed a new logo based on the imagery of my daughter's name (I've started dabbling in Mondrian, haha)
  • I removed a lot of redundant visual decoration and simplified the UI to suit my current taste
  • I care more about reader feedback, so I added Disqus for comments (Duoshuo, the old Chinese comment service, is long gone)

Also, the Jacman theme the old blog used is technically quite dated. I forked my own theme and started fixing the outdated or deprecated logic in it, for example gradually migrating the float layouts that were everywhere over to flex layouts.

Many choices can't be undone once made. Fortunately this one could. After going around the loop of third-party platform -> independent blog -> back to third-party platforms -> rediscovering how good an independent blog is, and back to an independent blog, I think I'll be staying on my independent blog for the long haul.

entry.title: Material Design: An Introduction and the Theory Behind It
entry.content:
material design
—— bringing science into art, so that people without much experience can still make decent designs

Introduction

The most accurate description is the official introduction1:

We challenged ourselves to create a visual language for our users that synthesizes the classic principles of good design with the innovation and possibility of technology and science. This is material design.
Develop a single underlying system that allows for a unified experience across platforms and device sizes. Mobile precepts are fundamental, but touch, voice, mouse, and keyboard are all ﬁrst-class input methods

Design principles

  1. Material is a metaphor:
    This metaphor is the foundation for understanding everything else in material design. Whenever you think about the material design space and about how a whole series of elements should move and behave, don't forget the metaphor behind it.

  2. Bold, graphic, intentional (that is, the design is arranged in advance; there is a deliberate motive behind it)
    It borrows the conventions of traditional print graphic design (typography, grids, space, scale, color, use of imagery) to guide visual treatment. These conventions don't just please the eye; they also serve to build hierarchy, convey meaning and direct focus (mostly in the sense of cognitive psychology, which I'll come to later).

  3. Motion provides meaning
    Animation is a very important part of front-end interaction, but material design doesn't use it arbitrarily. Its motion is abstracted from reality and matches users' cognitive patterns.

Below I'll unpack this official summary.

The "science and technology" behind Material Design

Drawing on traditional graphic design

The official introduction says material design "synthesizes the classic principles of good design with the innovation and possibility of technology and science." The "classic principles" part is easy to understand. Back in the age of print, people had already explored a great deal about how to present information in forms that are more pleasing and easier to take in, and had distilled a number of graphic design principles that work:

  • Consistency
  • Reducing memory load
  • Alignment, proximity
  • …
    These guidelines, originally for traditional paper media, were carried over to the new electronic media with very good results. Keep in mind that early web pages, apart from a few hyperlinks, came nowhere near the richness of presentation in print. Ideas from traditional graphic design gave web design very useful guidance, the grid system for example:

As the web developed, electronic media acquired something of their own. They were no longer purely static like paper; they had real "interaction." The web's new features needed other theoretical support. If we can no longer borrow from traditional graphic design, how do we create a set of design guidelines suited to these new web features? This is where the material design docs' "innovation and possibility of technology and science" comes in.

Opening up new design territory

If traditional graphic design can't be borrowed directly, look at whether there is something behind graphic design worth digging into. When looking for theoretical support, you need to search deeper in the reductionist direction. Roughly, that direction goes like this:

Design rests on psychology
Psychology rests on biology
Biology rests on chemistry
Chemistry rests on physics

These sweeping propositions are highly contested, but within these disciplines you can at least say they are "partly true." Digging deeper for design basically takes you as far as psychology and biology. Finding deeper theory gives a foundation for "creative" design. It lets the expression of the design space change, so you're no longer confined to transplanting traditional graphic design onto the new web medium; you can improvise freely from these deeper theories and create design forms suited to the web.

All that said, what exactly are these innovations and possibilities of technology and science?

Cognitive psychology

Before talking about cognitive psychology, here's a small example from Toutiao Quan (a social feature in the Toutiao news app):

This small example shows, to some extent, that cognition matters in front-end interfaces far more than people imagine, though many people don't realize how important it is.

The way humans come to know things (perception, learning, reasoning, memory and so on) follows certain fixed patterns, and people's cognitive behavior in front-end interfaces doesn't escape them. These patterns are formed by human biology. Since the Industrial Revolution, humans and their environment have been rapidly transformed, but evolution works on a scale of millions of years. The evolution of human biology was essentially finished long ago, and for the foreseeable future that biology will stay stable. Psychology already has quite a few findings that can teach design something:

  • How experience, environment and goals affect cognition
  • Gestalt phenomena in perception
  • Short-term and long-term memory
  • Research on reading behavior
  • The psychology of decision-making
  • …

All of the research listed above has applications in design. As for why we should talk about cognitive psychology at all, Designing with the Mind in Mind has a passage on it (slightly edited and expanded):

Following user-interface design guidelines isn't as step-by-step as following a cooking recipe. Design guidelines often describe goals rather than actions. They are deliberately very general so that they apply broadly, but that also means people often interpret their precise meaning, and how they apply to a specific design situation, in different ways.

To complicate things further, for any one design situation, several rules often seem to apply at once. That requires trade-offs between designs, and those trade-offs can't rest on the designer's personal taste alone; they need data and theory behind them. Data can come from the operations team.

Theory, though, can only come from the deeper level of cognitive psychology.

If you understand users' cognitive patterns, you're less likely to end up with something that "follows the design principles but doesn't match how users think," which makes for a bad user experience. In the example above, decorating the "…" follows quite a few design rules: it's more consistent, fits better with the other icons, stands out more, and so on. But it doesn't match cognition, and users easily make mistakes there.

Humans live in the physical world, while their minds sometimes roam the internet. This creates a "context switch" between the physical environment and the internet environment: people understand things on the internet through certain features of the real world, the trash can standing for the recycle bin, for example. With the help of psychology, we can make the cognitive transition from reality to internet design fairly smooth. The same goes for motion. Motion in the real world is smooth; nothing moves in broken lines (collisions aside). That's why smooth transitions look natural, and because of that naturalness they feel familiar and are more readily accepted.

Another place where a "context switch" happens is moving between scenes within an app. Transition animations need careful design to guide the eye, so that the transition feels natural and smooth and the user's train of thought doesn't break. This is where Bézier curves come into their own.

Biology

This is mainly research into the characteristics of biological structure, where cognitive psychology can look for its theoretical foundation, for example:

  • Neuroscience
  • Eye-tracking research
  • Research on how the eye forms images
  • This research is more fundamental and touches on evolutionary theory to some extent, so I won't go into it here. Here's one piece of theory about the eye's photoreceptor cells:

The spatial resolution of human vision drops sharply from the center to the periphery, for three reasons:

Pixel density
Each eye has 6 to 7 million cone cells, and they are packed far more densely in the center of the visual field (a tiny region called the fovea) than at the edges (corresponding to central vision). The fovea has about 158,000 cones per square millimeter, while the rest of the retina has only 9,000 cones per square millimeter (corresponding to peripheral vision).

Data compression
The fovea's cones connect 1:1 to ganglion cells, the starting point for processing and transmitting visual information, while in the rest of the retina several photoreceptors (cones and rods) connect to a single ganglion cell. In technical terms, peripheral visual information is compressed (lossily) before it reaches the brain, while central vision is not.

Processing resources
The fovea makes up only about 1% of the retina, yet 50% of the visual cortex is devoted to input from the fovea, and the other half processes data from the remaining 99% of the retina.

As a result, visual resolution at the center of our visual field is far higher than anywhere else. At arm's length, the fovea's field covers roughly the area of a thumbnail, about the width of three characters on the screen you're reading now. This is the basis of visual focus.

—— Jeff Johnson, Designing with the Mind in Mind (quotation slightly adapted)

Biological research on the eye tells us that when people look at a screen, their visual focus is basically only the size of a thumbnail; everything outside it is "peripheral vision." Given this mode of vision, how to guide the eye and draw users' attention to the information you want them to see is a real challenge. The most direct example is where and how an error message appears when an input field has an error.

Other things

Abstraction from physics && sensible quantification

The official material introduction also says "material is metaphor". Material is a metaphor. A metaphor for what?

What material design metaphorically refers to is a design material. Let's call it the "material card." It is abstracted from reality, stripped of reality's impurities and randomness, keeping spatial relationships, change and transition, and light and shadow. This material has thickness, and pieces of it have spatial relationships with one another. This actually hints at a bigger metaphor: the whole of material design stands for a particular design space, a space with three-dimensional structure, and material cards are the basic material it is built from.

Why go to so much trouble to abstract a design material and a virtual space?
Because materials, together with the rules for building with them, determine consistency

To understand this, we can start from architecture in the real world:

All design can be vividly described as "dancing in shackles," and this is especially obvious in architecture. Real-world architecture requires using basic available materials (brick, concrete, steel, glass) to produce designs that obey the physical laws of the real world.

Keep in mind that most buildings in the world are much alike. Only a few architects can design buildings that both obey the rules and rise above the ordinary.

If the materials and rules are too restrictive, the result is rigid expression. Although material design is abstracted from the real world, it also adds magical properties that don't exist in reality: material design cards can be freely split apart, merged, transformed and so on.

MD has some quantitative standards, and they provide design with a stronger layer of regulation:

  • Card thickness
  • Card elevation differences
  • Color choices
  • Animation timing
    • The longest gap between successive images that still lets them fuse visually: 20ms
    • The lag between a visual event and our complete perception of it: 100ms
    • The editing "window" for an event to enter consciousness: 250ms
    • …

This idea of "quantified design with a basis" is ahead of its time. It means design no longer belongs exclusively to masters with rich experience, and is no longer just bursts of inspiration and the expression of personal taste. If you know some history of science, you'll see why this act of "bringing science into design" at the level of design language matters. To draw a comparison: it is like bringing quantitative, scientific method into alchemy, which had always been practiced in mysterious ways, and it became chemistry.

Traces of combining science and technology can be seen in earlier design too, but none of them reformed and regulated design as thoroughly as material design does, through the form of a metaphorical space.
These features can be said to be why "people without much experience can still make decent designs."

People without much experience can still make decent designs?

What is decent design

  • Visually beautiful
  • Helps convey information precisely
  • Grounded in psychology and matched to users' cognitive habits (not just the designer's personal taste)
  • Material design has already built all of the above into its basic vocabulary, so doing front-end design with material design to some extent sets its floor: it won't be terrible.

Material Design tries to find a design point between art and science. That is possible, although it demands a great deal of the designer.

In my view, Material Design has partly achieved this. Its thinking is very clear and highly inspiring. Even if Material Design as a whole dissolves one day, many of its most inspiring ideas will carry on.

A Material Design mind map

The mind map above was compiled from the Material Design guidelines. The branches on the right describe Material Design's most basic components and structures. The branches on the left introduce some empirical best practices. Using what I've described above, readers can see whether they can find traces of these principles and techniques behind them.

References

Links:

material design official site
How should we understand Google's Material Design language? (Zhihu, Chinese)
The Verge's interview with Matias Duarte

Books

Grid Systems in Graphic Design
Designing with the Mind in Mind: Simple Guide to Understanding User Interface Design Guidelines
Don't Make Me Think

entry.title: The Metaphysics of Front-End Engineering (0)
entry.content:
Metaphysics... what I mean is, I want to talk about things beyond technology.
This post will be revised often.

Why I'm writing this

Front-end engineering is a peculiar profession. To borrow an elegant phrase, the front-end engineer is both painter and hacker. Along the product chain, front-end engineers sit between the server side and the designers, a bridge between engineering and design.

This means front-end engineers have to care not only about engineering but also about product design and user experience on the other end. Yet from what I see around me, many front-end engineers have built up far more on the engineering side than on the other.

This series introduces some of the more "humanistic" knowledge in front-end engineering, and it tries to cover only the parts where the humanistic can be explained with reason.

Explaining the humanistic with reason?

Take the relationship between design and psychology as an example:

Biology is grounded in chemistry, and chemistry is grounded in physics

In the natural sciences, one idea has had a far-reaching influence: reductionism. The sentence above roughly means that all biological phenomena can ultimately be traced back to the various chemical phenomena inside organisms, and all chemical phenomena can be traced back to the combinations and motions of various particles.
Reductionism is highly contested, but judging by the history of the natural sciences, it has been the most effective intelligible approach to research, producing a great many results through reductive analysis, and so it has been borrowed by other social disciplines (psychology, economics).
Modern psychology is barely a hundred years old. From the 1960s and 70s on, advances in medical technology and experimental methods, such as the arrival of EEG (electroencephalography) and MRI (magnetic resonance imaging), drove rapid progress in fields like cognitive psychology and neuropsychology, and also gave psychology a foundation that supports reductionism.

Psychology is grounded in biology

This sentence may be more contested, but following the reductionist line of thinking, at least some phenomena can be pushed one step further down to the level of biology.

The psychological foundations of design

Carrying the analogy all the way down, some parts of design can also find more universal psychological grounding, for example the alignment, proximity, contrast, and so on proposed in many design principles. This gives design a "universal explanatory foundation," so that design no longer looks like merely the expression of a designer's personal taste. When there are disagreements over a design, you can find a more relaxed way to settle them (relaxed compared with validating through data such as A/B tests): let's reduce it one level down and see what that says.

The plan

Roughly: design psychology, then information media, then philosophy of technology.
My knowledge is limited. Discussion and criticism is welcome.

entry.title: Front-End Metaphysics (1): Why Users Can't See the Favorites Button
entry.content:
This post looks at an application of cognitive psychology to the "Neihan Duanzi" app (a ByteDance joke-and-meme app; a little plug for my company's product).

The Neihan Duanzi operations team keeps getting user feedback asking "Does Neihan Duanzi have a favorites feature?", so much of it that you can't help wondering: why can't so many users see the "Favorite" and "Save" features? They sit right there on the panel that pops up when you tap Share, and by rights should be visible at a glance.

This is in fact a form of blindness known in psychology. Of course, once you know the two features exist and consciously look for them, the blindness disappears. But for many users that is a hard step to take. This post analyzes this baffling problem from the angle of cognitive psychology and proposes solutions.

The short version

A two-step analysis

Before the share panel opens, the share icon carries a strong goal cue (namely, sharing), which makes people subconsciously assume that every function in the panel that appears after tapping it is about sharing.

The Neihan Duanzi share icon:

Once the panel is open, attention, shaped by that goal, stays on the sharing functions, which leaves people blind to everything else. The function icons at the bottom also look very much like the iOS system style, which makes the blindness worse. (The image below is the panel after tapping; note the "Favorite" and "Save" functions at the bottom.)

What the user actually sees is this (the user only sees two spots: the top one when sharing, and the bottom one when cancelling. The middle part usually gets a quick sweep of the eye and is ignored):

How to fix it

It's actually simple. There are two directions:

  1. Replace the share icon with "…" (meaning more functions): for this icon, users expect several functions to choose from once it opens, so they will look through it more carefully.
  2. Keep the share icon for sharing only and split it out on its own (one icon, one function, as users expect), and put everything else under "…" (more functions).

Whichever direction you take, the style of the "Favorite", "Save" and other function icons needs to change so they don't look so close to the system's, ideally matching Neihan's own style.

For those who want to dig into the analysis, read on for the full version. It works mainly from a few theories of cognition and includes some quite interesting ideas from current cognitive psychology. Recommended.

The full analysis

Two questions (wish I could add a poll here)

  1. Have you ever noticed "Neihan Duanzi's Favorite and Save features"?
  2. If you have, how long after you started using the app did it take you to notice?

To describe the complete mental process of a user using Neihan Duanzi, I've included my own experience of using the app. If you're not interested, skip this section and go straight to the next major heading.

Background: my experience with the app

As of today I've been using the Neihan Duanzi app for about half a year. What puzzled me most was that sometimes I'd come across a picture or joke I really liked and wanted to save or favorite it, but couldn't find any feature for it.

As an engineer I consider myself very experienced with apps, yet I genuinely never found anything like that. In the end I could only guess the PM had left these two features out for some special reason. And to keep the jokes I liked, I had to share them straight to my own WeChat, as shown below (dumb, but I couldn't find a better way):

Today, at my first requirements meeting on Neihan, this question came back to me, so I asked the person in charge, and was told the "Favorite" and "Save" features do exist; I just hadn't found them. (Most people try to find something a few times without success, then basically give up and use some other workaround.)

So I went through every icon I could see, one by one. Sure enough, I finally found a few features I had overlooked for nearly half a year. For some reason they had been invisible to me, even though I had tapped the share icon countless times. As shown below, Favorite and Save are right there at the bottom of the panel:

Why were "Favorite" and "Save" invisible?

The reasons can be found in cognitive psychology. In short there are four main ones (I won't expand on them, just the conclusions):

The area where our gaze is focused (central vision) is very narrow. At normal screen distance (half an arm to an arm's length), our point of focus is roughly the size of a thumbnail.
Human attention is very limited. When looking at a phone, an ordinary person can basically focus on only one point (usually the point of gaze).
Attention is easily guided by goals. Things strongly related to the goal get noticed easily; the rest tends to be ignored.
How we perceive things is shaped by experience and habit.

Step-by-step analysis

Tapping the share icon

The share icon:

Anyone with experience of internet products knows this icon well, and usually taps it only when they want to share. Note the causality here: people generally don't tap the icon first and then decide whether to share. They come with the purpose from the start.

The share icon is so common that it sets up a strong representation (and a strong cue): the icon is the function. For experienced internet users, the share icon and the share function map one to one. (If functions other than sharing show up, that goes against what users expect.)

Taken together, these two points determine what users expect when tapping this icon: they're heading for sharing, and they expect to see sharing functions on the next screen (points 3 and 4 of the cognitive theory above).

Entering the share panel

The function panel:

Once in the share panel, because the user already has a goal and expectation and is shaped by them, their gaze and attention look like this (per the theory above, the user's point of focus is small, and it only lands on what most deserves attention), as below:

If the user decides not to share after all, habit sends their eyes straight to the bottom. Their gaze and attention at that moment look like this:

Another reason for the blindness
The Toutiao share panel && the Neihan share panel

Toutiao (ByteDance's news app):

Neihan:

Comparing the two, you can see that the buttons in the lower part of Neihan's share panel are styled very much like iOS, and this style uses light-gray line icons with very low visual salience (hard for peripheral vision to pick up). Drawing on their own experience of iOS, users subconsciously assume this part is just a bunch of miscellaneous built-in system functions, so their eyes sweep straight past it and the information is lost.

How to fix it

It's actually simple. There are two directions:

Replace the share icon with "…", meaning more functions, because for this icon users expect several functions inside once it opens, so they will look through it more carefully.

Keep the share icon for sharing only and split it out on its own (one icon, one function, as users expect), and put everything else under "…" (more functions).

Whichever direction you take, the style of the "Favorite", "Save" and other function icons needs to change so they don't look so close to the system's, ideally matching Neihan's own style.

entry.title: One Year After Graduation
entry.content:
One Year After Graduation

I still remember how lost I felt when nearly twenty years of school came to an end, and my first sleepless night in the rented flat in Longze seems like only yesterday. Yet in the blink of an eye, a year has passed since graduation.

Work

It still gnaws at me that I missed the interview round of the graduate entrance exam in philosophy by a single point. In the end, right before graduation, I went back to the computer industry.

Looking back, I've never written a single word about that time preparing for the exam. Maybe my thoughts were buried under a year of busy work and I never found the time. From the summer after my junior year, I put all my energy into preparing for the philosophy of science exam. Those were probably the fullest days of my four years in college: every day in the library, going from ancient Egypt and Mesopotamia to ancient Greece, then Rome, the Islamic world and early modern Europe. I learned about the course of science, the development of philosophy, the rise of modern philosophy of science and philosophy of technology, and the differences between Eastern and Western civilizations. I still clearly remember the stomachache in the exam room and the slightly over-the-top post I put on WeChat Moments when the exam ended. But in the end I fell at the gates of Peking University. I made my compromise with reality and with my age, and that was the end of me and philosophy of science as a field. Still, the way of thinking that philosophy of technology gave me has become part of how I think, and it will keep benefiting me in daily life and at work.

Feeling uneasy, I started job hunting and went to a startup founded by an upperclassman from my school. I don't know whether it was my own ignorance or the company trusting me too much, but on my very first interview I was hired on the spot. Later this even led to some arguments with family and friends. Young and reckless indeed. I also had a doubt that, looking back now, sounds a bit like showing off: everyone says finding a job is hard, so what's going on here? But I didn't think much about it. Graduation was pressing, I joined the company and began life as a workplace rookie, and the graduation trip I had planned was canceled.

I think I was still lucky. Because I'd spent the summer after junior year and almost all of senior year preparing for the exam, I had nearly zero internship experience in computing, and when I ran into real projects I was badly stretched. But I got good guidance at the company and gradually came to be valued quite a bit, and things slowly improved. That was how I spent a hard but upbeat half year. During those six months I really had the fearlessness of a newborn calf: I dared to voice all kinds of opinions and ideas, and my efforts to help the company build its own wiki and proper engineering management did make a difference. Being recognized by a platform may be the rarest thing you get from a job.

After six months, the company's business focus gradually became clear. It dropped the original startup project and concentrated on crowdsourcing services. But that direction was too far from my own plans, work fell into a loop, it felt more and more boring, and I even had some very strange arguments with the tech lead. In the end I jumped to Toutiao and began my career at a second company, but that's another story.

In terms of skills, I went from half ops, half backend when I first started, to backend, and then to frontend. I've touched more or less the whole web stack, and in the end I chose frontend as my personal breakthrough point. I chose it because the frontend is close to users; it's the place in the computer industry closest to users, and perhaps also the most humanistic place. I've always believed that philosophy of technology can contribute something to the internet industry, and the easiest place to bring them together is the frontend.

Life

This year I moved from Zhichunlu to Longze, and then from Longze back to Zhichunlu, as if completing a full circle.

When you live in a city like Beijing, rent is always a topic, and it comes down to one word: expensive. But since I'd started living my own life, I didn't want to do what my parents' generation did when they worked away from home, renting any old run-down place and just making do. So I went to Longze to share a place with friends and tried to create the kind of atmosphere you see in Friends. That turned out to be not very realistic, but it felt pretty good.

When I first moved into the rented flat, to borrow a saying from my hometown, I "couldn't get a grip on anything." I had to call my mom for advice, and she said it was because I lacked the basic household things. Little by little I bought pots, pans and bowls, and thanks to a kind and capable girlfriend, the place slowly got sorted out and started to feel lived in.

Cooking for myself and having friends over for dinner happened now and then in the first half of the year after moving in, but in the second half I was swamped with all sorts of things and got much lazier in my spare time; everything was basically waiting to be picked up again. Moving back to Zhichunlu was a big turning point. No more squeezing onto the subway and buses every day, and I had a lot more time, so I found the feeling of living again.

Mind

Over a year, a lot changes inside you. Some of the shortcomings from my student days were gradually made up for, and at the same time many good qualities slowly faded away, such as spending time studying every day and the fearlessness of a newborn calf.

Afterword

I wrote this in June, during graduation season. Because I switched computers in the middle, my train of thought kept getting interrupted, and it's still incomplete even now. But as I've gained experience at the new company, I've slowly found my way back into a learning state, and that feeling of not yielding even to my teachers when it comes to what's right. I've also got a somewhat more mature plan for my career ahead. To be continued.

entry.title: Topological Sort: Resolving JavaScript Module Dependency Order
entry.content:
Topological Sort

When I first heard the term "topological sort", I drew a complete blank. I ran through everything in my head and found nothing related to it. I'd studied graph algorithms as an undergraduate, but that mostly focused on graph connectivity, spanning trees, depth-first search, breadth-first search and so on. There didn't seem to be any "topological sort".

Only after learning what it basically is and where it's used did I realize that it had been there all along; I just hadn't clearly recognized the concept or its importance.

Module Dependencies in JavaScript

Anyone who writes JavaScript has probably run into the concept in the title. For example, there's a module A that depends on modules B, C and D; module B in turn depends on C, E and F; module C depends on D, E, F and G.

Put another way:

// module: {dependencies}
A: {B, C, D}
B: {C, E }
C: {D, E}
D: {E}
E: {}

If you're asked to write a program that computes the dependencies of every module in a system of interdependent modules, with the final output shown in the figure, how should you go about it?

Traversing the Graph Directly

Clearly, the module dependencies need to be converted into a graph data structure. Before I learned about topological sort, my instinct was that once the graph was built, I'd just pick a node, say A, start traversing from it, add every path A can reach, and merge them into A's dependencies. entry.title: Bricks, Stones, Web Standards and the W3C
entry.content:
Bricks and Stones

The humble brick is a marvel: on every street, down every alley, in every odd corner, practically anywhere people live, you can find it.
Stones are not as ubiquitous as bricks, but they hold a respectable place too: you see them in all sorts of building materials, sculptures, stone tablets and so on.

If I asked what the difference is between these two utterly ordinary things, bricks and stones, some people might laugh. Bricks and stones have nothing to do with each other. Apart from some overlap in what they are made of and some uses in construction, they have almost nothing in common, and discussing their differences seems even more pointless.

That answer isn't really wrong, but it isn't a good line of thought, or a good angle from which to look at the question. Let's look at how bricks and stones differ from one particular angle.

What's the Difference?

First difference: bricks are man-made, stones are natural.

At first glance there's nothing really wrong with this, but it doesn't give you an "oh, that's it" feeling either. We keep asking: so what?

Second difference: bricks conform to a specific size, stones have basically no fixed shape.

Since bricks are man-made, they must serve some predetermined purpose. Bricks are used to build houses, while unprocessed natural stones come in all sorts of odd shapes and are of little use in construction. But this difference also seems to be a true but useless statement.

Now the third difference: bricks embody industrial standardization, stones embody the disorder of nature.

Now this gets interesting, because following this line of thought we can find a lot. A brick is no longer just a brick; it is also part of the process of industrialization. It is precisely this industrial standardization that lets bricks be produced more easily and cheaply, organized more easily, and serve industry itself better.

A small brick basically distills the most important qualities of industry. Compare stones: with all their irregular shapes, they're good for little more than piling up a makeshift wall. If you want stones to play a bigger role, you have to process them the way bricks are made, so they can interact more easily with their surroundings.

So from this angle, although bricks and stones differ in themselves, the bigger difference lies not in the things themselves but in what shows up when you put them in a group.

So What?

You may think all of the above is right, but what does it prove? It doesn't seem to affect our lives. We may not be able to say exactly how bricks differ from stones, yet we already use them the right way.

Of course, the difference between bricks and stones is quite interesting even when examined in depth, but what's more interesting is the difference it contains between industrial standardization and non-standardization. This idea of industrial standardization has been everywhere since the industrial age: memory, hard drives and cases that follow specific rules let us assemble a personal computer easily. If you drive abroad on vacation and lose a wheel or a screw, you can buy a dozen more on the spot instead of fetching them from home. By contrast, imagine a world without standardization: if you had a custom car built in your hometown and it broke down halfway through a trip, picture how awkward that would be.

In fact, all industrial standardization means much the same thing: some standardization lets things fit better into a group, and some lets things exist beyond space, time and particular people.

Fitting into a group is what the bricks above do. Existing beyond space and time means that people in different places and different eras can all, by convention, use the same specification without worrying about compatibility. Existing beyond particular people means that once something is standardized, its manufacture, maintenance and reproduction no longer depend on a specific person or group. McDonald's and Chinese cooking are good examples. Chinese cooking depends on personal experience and is hard to quantify and standardize; if certain master chefs kick the bucket, you may never again eat dishes as good as theirs. McDonald's is different: as long as there are quantified recipes and standardized production, it hardly matters who drops dead.

Standardization is so common that it has become transparent and vanished from our view, a kind of "vanished existence."

Web Standards

Recently I came across a classic front-end interview question again: "How do you understand web standards and the W3C?" The line of thought here is basically the same as above: whatever industrial standardization brings, web standardization brings too.

I won't go into the details of web standards here. Web standards are of course good. They provide sound, practical standards for content, presentation and behavior, and on that basis you can build web system architectures that are highly available, easy to understand and highly adaptable.

W3C

The value of a standard shows only after it has spread and is followed. The more people follow it, the greater the benefit, until what you finally have is one standard web system after another running on the internet. Because every web system is standard, they are friendly not only to humans but also to the higher-level systems that process them (search engines, for example).

There is a rule of thumb about the internet: the value of the internet is proportional to the square of the number of nodes it is made of. Web standardization is similar. Web standards let you build web systems with a clear structure, and these standard web systems join together into a larger standard system. This makes all kinds of work easier to carry out and lets more be built on top, creating more value. At that point it is like the bricks discussed earlier, or the shipping containers I mentioned in an earlier post.

The value of the web standards themselves is not what matters most; there may well be better standards than the current ones. A well-defined standard that spreads easily can create more value than a better standard that is hard to spread. History is full of similar examples.

As for the W3C (the World Wide Web Consortium), it leads the web standardization process and is responsible for drafting and promoting web standards. It has to make sure not only that the current standards are good in themselves, but also coordinate different vendors so that the standards are easier to accept and spread. It has a heavy responsibility and a long road ahead.

entry.title: Clock Towers and the Revolution of Time
entry.content:
The clock, not the steam-engine, is the key-machine of the modern industrial age. — Lewis Mumford

The Clockmaker Who Beat Newton

I once happened to catch an episode of Luoji Siwei (a Chinese knowledge podcast) called "The Clockmaker Who Beat Newton." It tells the story of a clockmaker who built a highly accurate timepiece that made it possible to fix a ship's position at sea, giving a huge boost to navigation.

In fact, the story of clocks goes well beyond that. Determining longitude and advancing navigation was certainly a major event in human history, but compared with the role clocks played from the 10th to the 20th century, it is only the tip of the iceberg. It's just that the clock's other effects are almost "transparent" to us. Only after the philosophy of technology took shape did the veil slowly start to lift.

This post starts with the clock tower and briefly walks through some of the other stories of the clock, the spokesman for time.

Clock Towers Everywhere

Even today, we can still see clock towers in older big cities; they have long stood on university campuses and in churches. Even some newer cities put up a clock tower in a few key spots to remind people of the time.

The clock tower is a public timekeeping device. It appeared around the late 13th to early 14th century and quickly became a standard building in churches and universities. In monasteries and universities, people were required to arrange their daily activities strictly by the clock: prayers, services, meals and so on in a monastery all followed a strict rhythm and order.

In fact, if the clock tower was the product of people gathering into cities and needing to organize their lives and coordinate their activities, then monasteries already had timekeeping devices around the 10th century, well before clock towers appeared. Legend has it that a monk named Gerbert invented a mechanical water clock in the late 10th century. Regularity, order and punctuality were almost the natural requirements of monastic life, and they kept getting stronger over time. (See Lewis Mumford, Technics and Civilization.)

With the mechanical clock tower, timekeeping was no longer at the mercy of the weather. Water freezes, and the sun, moon and stars get covered up; a mechanical clock has none of these weaknesses and can run fairly reliably in all kinds of natural conditions. So it was quickly adopted by churches and monasteries, and later by the universities that emerged.

The meaning of the clock tower, and its disappearance
As mentioned above, the clock tower is a public timekeeping device, and it carries its own norms from birth: regularity, order, punctuality, and the quantification of time, something you can neither see nor touch.

A clock tower can coordinate and constrain human production and life over a wide area, so that all kinds of activities proceed in order. Inside churches and monasteries, its effect may have been strict prayers and services, a code of conduct in the religious sense. But once it left the church and entered the city, this clock-driven norm of punctuality and order coordinated human production and gradually brought the notion of time into the human world.

One effect of this notion of time is that it raises the efficiency of human production (before the "concept of efficiency" was born, efficiency itself already existed and was being strengthened, consciously or not). This in turn kept pushing the clockmaking trade forward.

A heavy timekeeping device like a clock tower usually served a whole large area, which was not very convenient. As clockmaking kept improving, especially after the invention of the mainspring in the 15th century, there was finally a technical basis for making clocks smaller. They shrank, and small table clocks began to enter people's homes. As clockmaking grew more precise and cheaper, this kind of timekeeping device began to spread.

The Revolution of Time

Some historians believe that in the centuries before the Industrial Revolution, another revolution had already been quietly under way: the so-called "revolution in the notion of time," or the "efficiency revolution." The changes it brought became the foundation of the Industrial Revolution.

The revolution of time can be traced, roughly, to the point when clocks became fully woven into human life. When people began to leave behind the primitive "relative notion of time," that is, sensing the passage of time entirely through the sun, moon, stars and the turning of the seasons, and adopted an artificial, mechanical means of keeping time, the revolution of time began. Time was no longer the unfolding and change of things; it became something independent, something that could be measured and quantified.

People began to mark time off according to the clock, ever more precisely. The introduction of hours, minutes and seconds made people clearly feel the passing of "time," and the important role time plays in daily life and in commerce. As commerce developed, producing more resources within a given time became an absolute pursuit. By then, the idea of "efficiency" had already begun to sprout.

People kept finding ways to raise efficiency: improving production processes, reforming production management, adopting new technologies, and so on. It was in this environment that the Industrial Revolution found soil in which to germinate.

Time Is Money

Today, "time is money" has become an everyday metaphor. In our culture, time has become a precious commodity, a limited resource we need to reach our goals.
