People are paid by the hour or the week, and phone calls are billed even more precisely, by the minute. We have borrowed a lot of money vocabulary to talk about time: time is something you can spend, waste, budget, invest, save or squander. In short, the notion of time has rebuilt the basic behavior of our daily lives and the way we understand the world.

All of this started with clock towers and other man-made timekeeping devices that run independently of nature.

entry.title: The reflective property of the ellipse: why light from one focus always reaches the other
entry.content:
I suddenly remembered an article about the optical property of the ellipse that I posted somewhere else a long time ago. Even today I find that explanation intuitive and fun. Back then I thought it was the "essential" explanation, but a classmate pointed out that "intuitive" is probably the more accurate word.

The article talks about ellipses, but the same idea applies more or less to conic sections in general.

The optical property of the ellipse

Among the properties of conic sections, you often see a picture like the one below: a ray of light leaving one focus of an ellipse reflects off the wall of the ellipse and passes through the other focus.

Other conic sections, such as the parabola and the hyperbola, have similar properties — they are all about what happens to light coming from a focus.

But why?

Of course you can prove it mathematically: at the point of reflection (P in the figure), the incoming ray and the outgoing ray make equal angles with the tangent at that point. I'll skip the proof here. It takes a few turns, but it's not hard to follow.

The problem is that after working through a pile of math, I still wasn't satisfied with the answer. To me, a mathematical proof just takes one step back into mathematics and restates the original problem in mathematical terms. I could keep asking: why such a coincidence — why do the angle of incidence and the angle of reflection come out exactly equal after the calculation?

What I wanted to know was "why does the ellipse have this property", not "prove that the ellipse has this property" — just as Wang Yin (a Chinese programming-language researcher and blogger) puts it in his essay on causes and proofs. What I'm really getting at is the difference between the efficient cause and the final cause.

So could I have predicted this in advance, without going through such a complicated proof?

A more interesting explanation (from mechanics)

I puzzled over this, and over all the curious properties of the ellipse, for a long time in high school.

Then one day I noticed how my math textbook said to draw an ellipse: fix a string to two nails, pull the string taut with the tip of a pen, and go once around the nails — the result is an ellipse.

Thinking about it carefully, this description is interesting because it carries two hidden facts.

The first is obvious, and is essentially the definition of the ellipse: for any point on the ellipse, the sum of its distances to the two foci is constant.

The second is subtler, and you can see it by looking at the drawing process physically: as you draw, at any point of tangency the forces from the two ends of the string on the pen tip are equal. So the angle of incidence must equal the angle of reflection — otherwise the string wouldn't be in balance (it would slide). From this you can foresee that the calculation will come out this way.

At that point the "why" finally had an "intuitive" explanation.

Some fun generalizations

The same reasoning extends to the other conic sections, and even the ellipse itself has some extensions — for example, changing the distance between the two nails. What happens when the two nails coincide? The answer is obvious.

entry.title: What Is a Modal Dialog? What "Modal" Actually Means
entry.content:
Where the Question Came From

While learning front-end development, I ran into a puzzling term: 模态框 ("modal box"), the Chinese name for the modal dialog, a special kind of pop-up window. For a while it was hard to say what exactly was special about it, or what fundamentally set this kind of pop-up apart from other windows. Unlike plain words such as "dialog" or "panel," the Chinese word 模态 ("modal") feels mysterious through and through. It's hard to get an intuitive sense of what it is or what the word is trying to express, and you can't help being confused: what on earth does "modal" mean?

With computing vocabulary, I've always held this belief: if a term feels mysterious, there must be more hidden behind it, perhaps a metaphor, perhaps some deeper design principle. Either way, the meaning behind such terms is worth investigating properly; these small words may turn out to be doorways into one fascinating world after another.

What Does "Modal" Mean?

To understand the modal dialog, besides looking at what the term actually refers to (you can try Bootstrap's modal component), the first thing to do is figure out what "modal" means.

**The Chinese 模态 translates the English word modal.**

First, the dictionary definitions of "modal": relating to mode, to modality, to form.

Then look at some baffling technical terms built from the word:

  • Modal analysis
  • Modal matrix
  • Modal logic
  • Modal dialog

Let's guess how the word was introduced, or rather how the English modal was rendered in Chinese. You want to express content in a particular state; how do you translate that? We know the word 模型 ("model") carries the sense of "a fixed abstraction of something," so it can express "a fixed pattern," and the word 状态 ("state") describes how something behaves in a given situation. Put the two together, and 模态 practically suggests itself. Of course, the actual translation and coinage must have been far more complicated than this, but the core idea is the same: how to express a concept faithfully, clearly and elegantly.

After this analysis, we can say we understand "modal" a little. It refers to a particular state.

Now look again at the technical terms above, and they become easier to understand: they all carry the sense of "studying things in some particular state."

What Is a Modal Dialog?

With that understanding of the word, we can move on to the concept of the modal dialog. Literally, it should mean "a window in a particular state."

Seen only this way, it may still be a little hard to grasp. That's because we're missing something: the context in which modal dialogs are used. Only by adding that can our understanding be complete.

So what is that context? The term arose in software, so let's first look at how software is normally used. When we use software, we usually proceed step by step along our own line of thought. Say we're using a shopping system: we follow the process in our heads based on our existing understanding of the software, choosing products, adding them to the cart, placing the order and paying. These processes can be called the "normal state" of using software.

The modal dialog, a "window in a particular state," is defined relative to this normal state. A modal dialog is a window in a particular state that interrupts us out of the normal state and focuses our attention on handling that particular state. Look at how a modal dialog actually behaves: when it appears, it blocks all other operations, and what the user can attend to is limited to the inside of the current modal dialog, unless you deliberately close it, end the interruption, and return to the original normal flow.

That is the core idea of the modal dialog. Strictly speaking, the modal dialog is a concept from UI design. Wikipedia defines it as follows:

model window

In user interface design, a modal window is a graphical control element subordinate to an application’s main window which creates a mode where the main window can’t be used. The modal window is a child window that requires users to interact with it before it can return to operating the parent application, thus preventing the workflow on the application main window. Modal windows are often called heavy windows or modal dialogs because the window is often used to display a dialog box.

Modal windows are commonly used in GUI systems to command user awareness and to display emergency states, although they have been argued to be ineffective for that use. Modal windows are prone to produce mode errors.

Of course, the modal dialog as a design idea implies coercion. It forces the user's attention out of their normal train of thought and onto the contents of the dialog, which amounts to forced thinking. This design is generally used for warnings about fairly dangerous operations.

But criticism of modal dialogs comes in many forms, mainly of this coercive design approach and of whether it should be replaced by better solutions. Some even declare modal dialogs "evil." For these criticisms, see the following:

  • Why are modal dialog boxes evil?
  • Never Use a Warning When you Mean Undo

"Modeless"

Where there is a concept of modal, there is of course a concept of modeless. I'll set modeless aside for now.

entry.title: HTML5 Design Principles — notes on Jeremy Keith's talk
entry.content:
The grand title comes from a talk. I find the way Jeremy Keith reasons in his keynote very close to how I like to think, and at the time there was no good Chinese version online, so I collected and tidied up a Chinese translation and reposted it on this blog.

A while ago our team kept arguing about whether an API should return UTC time strings or Unix timestamps. My position was "design for people first, then for machines", so I argued for the more readable UTC time.

The point of that example is that when we make a decision, we shouldn't just go with a passing thought and assume things should be a certain way. We should follow design principles that have clearly stood the test of time — especially when facing a hard trade-off.

Likewise, when we look at something new — HTML5, say (not that new anymore) — we shouldn't only look at its new elements and new APIs. We should think about the design philosophy and history behind it, and the pain points it solves. That's how we come to understand where these things come from.


The talk

The Chinese version of this post is a reposted translation of Jeremy Keith's keynote HTML5 Design Principles at Fronteers 2010 (October 21, 2010). Since the original is in English, read it in his own words: HTML5 Design Principles, by Jeremy Keith.

The talk walks through the principles behind HTML5:

  • Avoid needless complexity
  • Support existing content
  • Pave the cowpaths
  • Degrade gracefully
  • Priority of constituencies: put end users first

entry.title: Why We Should Ask "Why" When Learning Computer Science
entry.content:
Recently, while using Bootstrap, I ran into a design question about dropdown menus. Bootstrap's default dropdown component is built on a list as its HTML base rather than on <select></select>. I figured there must be some intent on the designers' part behind this, but for someone like me who has just started with front-end work, it was hard to dig into. After asking around, though, I found that people didn't seem to pay much attention to the design intent behind these implementations.

In an earlier post, open questions, I raised a question that went roughly like this: in the field of computing, why should we ask about the motivation behind something? Learning front-end development lately has given me a deeper feel for this question, so I'm pulling it out to discuss on its own.

The "Four Causes" in the Philosophy of Science

As early as ancient Greece, philosophers began pondering the nature of things. One very famous philosopher put forward a set of arguments explaining motion and change in things, and the core idea is what the heading above describes: the "four causes". And, as you'd expect, the philosopher's name is Aristotle.

To save time explaining the concept of the four causes, I'll excerpt a few paragraphs from Professor Wu Guosheng's (a Chinese historian and philosopher of science) blog post Heidegger's Philosophical Reflections on Technology. Of course, you can also consult the English Wikipedia entry, or more specialized books on the philosophy of science:

What brings a thing into appearance is called the cause of that thing. Aristotle held that there are four kinds of cause: the "material cause", the "formal cause", the "final cause", and the "efficient cause". Take the making of a crown: gold is its material cause; the shape of the crown is its formal cause; the emperor's use of it to hold grand ceremonies and display his majesty and splendor is its final cause; and the craftsman, who gathers all the requirements and preparations and does his part to finally bring the crown forth, is its efficient cause.

Today we don't really understand the doctrine of the four causes. We don't know why four causes were proposed, much less why exactly these four. Because when we speak of a "cause", what we usually mean is only the thing that acts directly and produces and brings about the final result, which is only the efficient cause in Aristotle's sense (it can also be called the "proximate cause" —note by the quoter). For the crown as something made, from our point of view today, the craftsman is its only cause.

The efficient cause became the decisive one among the four, and ultimately determined how causality is defined. This happened after the 16th and 17th centuries (that is, the years when the mechanical view of nature was taking shape —note by the quoter), and it was extraordinary: it contained modern thought's exclusion of the final cause. The appearance of a thing came to be described as the result of another, earlier thing plus some acting force; in a sense, the thing became something ready-made, so-called "matter". Things no longer "come to" appear; they are simply present, permanently present. Causality no longer speaks of what makes a thing "appear", but of quantitative changes in matter that is fundamentally present.
This definition of causality makes it impossible for us to understand the Greek doctrine of the four causes. In particular, it stamps our understanding of the efficient cause in the Greek doctrine with the brand of our own era: acting on a thing so as to change it. But the inner connection among the four causes in the Greek sense is completely lost. Heidegger reminds us that understanding the essence of instruments depends on understanding the essence of causality, and we remain utterly ignorant of the essence of causality to this day, an ignorance shown especially in our misunderstanding of the Greek four causes.

Professor Wu's text above already explains quite clearly what the four causes are, and why today, when we mention the "cause" of something, the implied context is "one cause" rather than "four causes". This comes from the paradigm shift in the view of nature that took place in the 16th and 17th centuries. That shift treated the "efficient cause" among the four (which can also be called the proximate cause) as the primary factor in how things change, while the other causes faded into the background.

The Efficient (Proximate) Cause: An Effective Way of Inquiry in Traditional Natural Science

In traditional science, when we talk about the cause of something, we usually mean its proximate cause. Take a question I once answered on Zhihu (a Chinese Q&A site similar to Quora): Why is ethanol non-toxic, while methanol, propanol and butanol are all toxic?

Then look at the answers below it. The top-voted answer describes the molecular structure of alcohols and their corresponding chemical properties, as well as the different effects that different alcohols have inside the human body, and gives a quite professional answer. What it sets out from this angle is "the proximate cause of alcohol toxicity", that is, "how things currently are".

Since the Scientific Revolution, the thinking reflected in that answer has been the guiding idea of research in the natural sciences. This mode of inquiry, asking after the "proximate cause", has an enormous advantage: it leads humanity to set aside the most fundamental questions for the time being, concentrate on what can be studied at the current stage, and stay silent about what can't be studied or is temporarily out of reach. For example, to study the motion of objects, the most direct approach is to study the forces that push them and the different effects produced under different forces, while setting aside what Newton called the first mover and not considering it for now. It is precisely by advancing step by step, precisely, according to an internal logic, and accumulating continuously, that this form of research has achieved major results, as we can see.

But this doesn't give "our expectation" an explanation that feels more fundamental. Yes, the answer is very accurate and fits very well with the physiological and chemical knowledge humans currently have, but on that basis one can still ask: why is it like this? What caused this physiological and chemical state of affairs?

The Final Cause: Our Expectation

As the question at the end of the previous section suggests, we humans always psychologically want a "more fundamental" explanation, and somewhat stubbornly believe that "a more fundamental explanation ought to exist", even though for now many of these are just "illusions of causality". This shows up even more clearly in Darwin's theory of evolution, as in my answer to the question "Why is ethanol non-toxic, while methanol, propanol and butanol are all toxic?":

This is obviously a question of physiology plus evolution, and once evolution is involved, "causality" gets subtle.

When we say something is "toxic", there's an implied context: toxic to living things. Methanol, ethanol, propanol and butanol are structurally similar, so why is ethanol the least toxic? Answering from physiology and chemistry can only tell you "what" this toxicity looks like. In terms of causality, reasoning this way finds the "proximate cause" of "being toxic".

The "proximate cause" is the cause most directly related to the thing being studied. Looking for proximate causes is also the most common form of research in physics and chemistry. Its origin has a lot to do with the Scientific Revolution of the 16th and 17th centuries; the details are complicated, so I won't go into them here.

But in biology, studying only proximate causes explains "how it manifests, what it is like" well, but doesn't explain "why it is like this" well. In answering "what it is like", physiology and chemistry have done a fine job. As for "why it is like this", we can only turn to evolution.

My bold guess is this: ethanol occurs more readily under natural conditions (why it occurs more readily is another question), so living things have had more opportunities to come into contact with ethanol than with other alcohols. This has made life less sensitive to ethanol.

As for evidence, all I can say is that this guess is consistent with the logic of evolution. Producing concrete data would be hard.

Setting aside for now whether this answer is correct, and also not worrying about the headache-inducing causality in evolution, what I want to say is that even a "half-baked final-cause answer" like the one above gives us a feeling of "Ah, that's it!", as if it satisfied some longing deep in our souls.

This is in fact the charm of the "final cause": it satisfies a certain mysterious human craving for the truth, even when the final cause is sometimes illusory.

The "Final Cause" in Computer Science

The above describes the way of researching or learning in the traditional natural sciences. But computer science is different. In nature, all kinds of things exist independently of humans, and most of them existed countless years before humans did. It is hard, one could even say basically impossible, for us to trace back and see what things looked like when they first appeared, and where they sat within the complex system of nature.

In computing it's a completely different story. A great deal of it is "created by humans". These things were built out of certain motives, which matches human intuition very well: if it's done this way, there must be a "more fundamental reason" behind it, and that fundamental reason is the creator's purpose and intent.

This can basically be generalized to everything related to man-made things. Whenever we design or create something, there is some purpose in it rooted in the environment of the time. Take ordinary tables and chairs: every design carries the purpose its creator wanted to express. None of them appeared out of nowhere; they come accompanied by the intentions the creator planted in them. With a folding chair, the designer may have been thinking about saving space. With a chair built purely with mortise-and-tenon joints, the creator may have been after naturalness and environmental friendliness, or nostalgia for days gone by.

In computing, we should likewise ask about the "final cause" of something, that is, the original intention of the creator behind it. By asking about these original intentions, we can better understand the intent built into a thing and deepen our understanding of it. Take design patterns: why do these design patterns exist, and are there others? Once we understand this, we realize these things aren't set in stone, and that frees up our creativity.

Front-End Development

This is even more true in front-end development. The front end is purely a human construction, so there are many things we can ask about. For example, what is HTML5 for? Why was HTML5 proposed, and what were its proposers thinking?

Asking these questions lets us trace a problem back to the designers' intent and understand the original purpose, which in turn gives us a deeper understanding and a better grasp of what's to come.

entry.title: What Is a Metaphor, and How Is It Different from a Simile?
entry.content:
Metaphor

Why Clear Concepts Matter So Much

In American TV shows we often hear characters mention or use the rhetorical device called "metaphor," and we vaguely know it is similar to "analogy," but we lack a clear understanding of it. In fact, we often use this device unconsciously in everyday conversation, and the reason it stays unconscious is that we have no clear concept of "metaphor."

It is not only metaphor. In daily life we often run into situations like this: before you have a clear concept of something, you don't pay it much attention even if it is around you all the time. Your awareness of it is in an "unconscious" state. Once you grasp the concept, you leave that muddled unconscious state, start deliberately noticing it around you, and are surprised to discover: oh, it was there all along.

To put it more philosophically, this is "being as non-being, the nothing that exists." From experience, humans build a concept of a thing in language, and that linguistic concept in turn makes us pay more attention to the corresponding thing, which finally deepens our understanding of both the concept and the thing.

In The Non-Designer's Design Book, Robin Williams opens with the story of the Joshua tree. She was given a book on identifying trees one Christmas, read that the Joshua tree could be recognized from just two clues, and decided from its odd-looking photo that she had certainly never seen one in her parents' neighborhood. When she walked outside with the book, she found Joshua trees in front of most of the houses on the street, where she had lived for years without ever noticing them. Her point: once you can name something, you notice it everywhere, and it becomes yours.

What this example describes is not a special case; behind it lie deeper questions about language and cognition. Concepts are the most basic units of thought, and we can hardly overstate their importance. Some work in cognitive science and linguistics now studies exactly these questions. This post briefly introduces the concept of "metaphor" and explains why metaphor matters in computer science.

I originally introduced metaphor inside another post, but I came to feel the concept was so important that it needed a post of its own. As described above, once the concept of "metaphor" is clear, you begin to leave your old unconscious use behind and consciously use this device to express concepts and things that were hard to put into words. You will also find that metaphor is everywhere and come to appreciate deeply the benefits it brings.

How Code Complete Treats Metaphor

In Code Complete, right after the welcome chapter, Steve McConnell introduces metaphors for software development and stresses their importance. He observes that computer science has the most colorful vocabulary of any field: walk into a carefully climate-controlled machine room and you will find viruses, Trojan horses, worms, bugs, logic bombs, crashes, flames, twisted sex changers and fatal errors. Where else would you run into all that?

These vivid metaphors describe particular phenomena and things in the software world, and lively metaphors like these can describe much broader phenomena too. With their help we can understand the process of software development more deeply.

So What Is a Metaphor?

A metaphor is a kind of figurative comparison. In Chinese the word literally means "hidden comparison," in contrast to the ordinary, explicit comparison, the "simile."

By comparison, the simile is the form of figurative comparison used most in everyday speech, as in Chinese stock phrases like "as beautiful as a flower" or "a father's love is like a mountain." We use similes mainly for aesthetic reasons: we want to add the aesthetic qualities of one thing to another. In the phrases above, we want to give a person the loveliness of a flower, or give a father the weight and towering steadiness of a mountain.

A metaphor is different. It is mostly used not for aesthetic reasons but to express some real connection between two things. Take Shakespeare's famous metaphor:

All the world's a stage,
And all the men and women merely players;
They have their exits and their entrances; and one man in his time plays many parts…
—William Shakespeare

Shakespeare does not use this metaphor to give the world and people the aesthetic qualities of a stage and actors. He genuinely believes that the way the world works resembles the way a stage play works in certain respects.

Many people (usually cognitive linguists) believe that metaphor has cognitive significance. In other words, it can help humans understand something better, and the means it uses is to connect a newer, unfamiliar concept to other concepts that are already known and easier to understand, using the similarity between the two to aid understanding.

Some Examples: Metaphors We Have and Haven't Noticed

In language, when something new appears and needs a word to name it, one approach is to extend an existing word. This extension is not arbitrary; there is usually some particular similarity between the new thing and the old one.

Some typical examples:

  • socket: originally a plug or electrical socket. In computer communication it was extended to mean a mechanism for exchanging information, and like a wall socket it carries the sense of plugging two ends together.
  • docker: originally a dock worker. Today there is a widely used virtualization technology called Docker. It also borrows the metaphors of dock workers and shipping containers to express standardized delivery.
  • To be continued

entry.title: A Running Log of Problems and Fixes
entry.content:
Meta: This post records problems I run into day to day, along with their solutions.

Miscellaneous

Running scheduled commands with Linux crontab + Django commands

The problem

While building an archive management system, I had a task that needed to periodically pull data from a DB2 database, process it, and store it in MySQL. That meant running a standalone script inside Django that uses Django's environment.

The solution

Django provides user-defined custom commands for exactly this:

Writing custom django-admin commands¶

And Linux provides a handy tool for scheduling tasks:

linux crontab

Error 2006 'mysql server has gone away' when writing large amounts of data to MySQL

The problem

While building an archive management system with Django + MySQL, this error appeared when I wrote nearly 30,000 rows into MySQL in one go.

The solution

It turned out MySQL has a default limit on the size of data written. Just add the following to /etc/my.cnf (create the file yourself if it doesn't exist):

[mysqld]
max_allowed_packet = 16M

Of course, you can also solve this by limiting how much data you write to MySQL at a time.

Vim split screens and the Ctrl P plugin

I'd always heard how great the ctrl p plugin was. But when I first tried it, I really didn't see what was so powerful about it, until I later discovered Vim's split-screen feature.

Using Vim's split screens together with Ctrl P lets me open multiple files without leaving Vim, which saves a huge amount of time spent cd-ing around directories on the command line.

Reference: Vim's split-screen feature

Basic regular expressions

Once I needed to pad a bunch of short lines of text with trailing spaces so that every line had the same width.
At first I tried all kinds of column editing and block editing, and none of it worked. Did I really have to write a program just for this?

Later I found that a regular expression pretty much does the job:

%s/$/ n_spaces /g

In Vim, the $ symbol has a rich set of meanings; here it refers to the character just before the end of the line.

Front end

Mainly notes on things that are easy to confuse while learning front-end development. Personally, among HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, CSS is by far the hardest to pin down. Because of browser default styles and constraints, CSS inheritance, cascading rules, and so on all acting together, CSS often doesn't behave the way I expect. So there may be more CSS content here.
These are just scattered notes; for now I don't have the energy to organize them into standalone posts. Maybe later I'll expand some of the expandable bits into proper articles.

The difference between CSS pseudo-classes and pseudo-elements

Pseudo-classes
Pseudo-elements

Telling the concepts apart

An answer on Stack Overflow:
What is the difference between a pseudo-class and a pseudo-element in CSS?

The explanation on W3C:
pseudo-elements
pseudo-classes

Inheritance of relative font-size values in CSS

When font-size uses relative units like em, the calculations compound.

From Stylin' with CSS (quoted from the Chinese edition)

Generally, em uses the browser default as its base unit, that is, 1em = 16px. If you want to use em but also need to set specific pixel sizes, you can set the body's font-size to 62.5%. That changes the base size from 16 pixels to 10 pixels (16 × 62.5% = 10). Then the correspondence between em and pixels becomes very clear: 1em equals 10 pixels, 1.5em equals 15 pixels, 2em equals 20 pixels, and so on.

The p element's text is 12 pixels (the body's 16-pixel base × .75 = 12px). strong is a child of p, so its relative text size compounds level by level, and it should be 16px × 0.75 × 0.75 = 9px.

Note the difference from text-indent: font-size compounds, whereas with text-indent a later value overrides the earlier one.

text-indent is inherited by child elements. If you set text-indent on a div, all paragraphs in the div inherit that indent value. However, as with all inherited CSS values, the indent value is not the value set on the ancestor but the computed value. Here is an example.

Suppose a 400-pixel-wide div contains text indented 5%; the indent is then 20 pixels (5% of 400). Inside this div is a 200-pixel-wide paragraph. As a child element it inherits its parent's text-indent value, so its text is indented too. But what is the inherited indent value? Not 5%, but 20 pixels. That is, the child inherits the indent value computed from the parent's width. As a result, even though the paragraph is only half as wide as its parent, its text is still indented 20 pixels. This ensures that paragraphs are indented by the same distance no matter how wide they are. Of course, setting text-indent on the child element overrides the inherited value.

How inline-block behaves

This value causes an element to generate an inline-level block container. The inside of an inline-block is formatted as a block box, and the element itself is formatted as an atomic inline-level box.

Put more plainly: an inline-block element has both the block element's ability to have its width and height set and the inline element's default behavior of not breaking onto a new line. And that's not all; for example, an inline-block element can also take the vertical-align property. In short:
an inline-block element is a block container formatted as an inline element.

Open question:

Does an inline-block's margin push out the parent's height, while an ordinary block's margin collapses with the parent's margin?

References:
The past and present of inline-block

w3c: the ‘display’ property

mozilla: vertical-align

Using rem

Today I experimented with the rem relative unit in Chrome. My initial test code was:

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<head>
    <meta charset="utf-8">
    <title>test rem</title>
    <style type="text/css">
        html{
            font-size: 62.5%;  // the behavior here is a bit odd
        }
        body{
            font-size: 1.2rem;
        }
        div{
            width: 300px;
            height: 300px;
            background-color: red;
            padding: 1rem;
        }
    </style>
</head>
<body>
    <p>测试字体大小</p>
    <div></div>
</body>
</html>

But at this point font-size was not 10px. I'd seen online that people set the root element's font-size to 10px to make later calculations easier, but here it didn't seem to take effect.

The reason is that Chrome's default minimum font size is 12px; any value set below that gets reset to 12px. In that case 1rem=12px. On Chrome's minimum font size limit,

see: What happened after Chrome dropped -webkit-text-size-adjust

Block-level and inline elements

  • Block-level elements
    • Take up a whole line
    • width and height can be set
    • Default
  • Inline elements
    • Setting width and height has no effect

Reference: The few most essential concepts in CSS

width and height

Defines the width of an element's "content area." The default value is auto, and it is not inherited. The browser computes the actual width.

When height and width use percentage relative units, they are calculated relative to the parent element's width (the parent's width works the same way). If not specified, the default is the image's own width and height; if the image fails to load, the alt attribute value is shown, or the browser's built-in broken-image display.

When to use each centering method

// Horizontal centering
// When using margin to center an element horizontally,
// you need to specify the width of the element being centered (it has nothing to do with the parent's width)
// Obviously this only applies to block-level elements
// It centers the element the property is set on, not its children or its parent
margin: 0, auto;   
text-align： center

How things behave when an inner box is bigger than its outer box can contain

Tools I've used

  • reactjs react router
  • underscore
  • project-path (npm module)
  • fixed-data-table (React component)

Over-engineering in code

What is over-engineering in code

Over-design, or over-engineering, means exactly what it says: when writing code, imagining too many scenarios that don't actually exist and designing for those imagined scenarios, such as constantly accounting for changes that might come in the future. In reality, the code at that point is still a long way from needing to consider any of that.

Over-engineering I've run into

When we were building a product before, we actually overemphasized possible future risks or changes in some places. For example, the product stored images on Qiniu cloud storage (a Chinese cloud storage provider), and at first everything was stored as URLs. But then an engineer imagined a scenario: "What if Qiniu's domain changes someday, or we stop using Qiniu?" So he set about changing the URLs to keys, only to find that the rewrite wasn't easy at all, and in the end it was abandoned.

The other case was over-design at the product level. While we were developing a product, the product manager's prototype changed countless times, and some of the last changes even altered the most basic data, rendering all the code we'd written completely useless. And this was precisely a product that needed fast iteration; to this day the first version still isn't done. Strictly speaking this example isn't over-design, but I'll put it here for now.

I don't understand how we, who are always going on about the MVP (minimum viable product), completely ignored it when building our own product.

Of course, for someone like me without much programming experience, it's still too early to be thinking about this. I'm just writing it down for now, to reflect on later.

Product experience

First impressions of iOS

My Nexus, after three years of service, finally got too old and decrepit and was honorably discharged. Torn by Android's endless variety, I ended up just getting an iPhone. Right away a few things felt really awkward. Some of that is naturally the unfamiliarity that comes with switching systems, but some of it is clearly bad design.

The useless pull-down menu

Compared with Android's powerful pull-down menu, iOS's pull-down menu is only used for notifications or recently used app features, and part of the settings is placed in a menu that slides up from the bottom. Even those settings are incomplete. Take Wi-Fi: you can only toggle it on and off, and can't use it as an entry point to configure Wi-Fi further. To configure Wi-Fi you have to go dig through the Settings app.

Now look at Android's pull-down menu: whether it's Wi-Fi or the flashlight, it's incredibly practical and convenient, and used very frequently.

The infuriating alarm settings

This one is even more obvious. On Android, setting an alarm takes one step. On the iOS alarm page, you first tap Edit in the top left to enter edit mode, then tap the time before you can choose it. A feature that could be done in one step gets stubbornly split into several. Using it is incredibly frustrating.

The baffling keyboard and system-wide copy and paste

The key proportions on the 9-key input layout are a real pain: the main area doesn't get enough space, while a big confirm button sits on the right, taking up a ton of room.

And the behavior of the keyboard and system-wide copy and paste is simply bewildering; there's no discernible pattern to any of it. It feels like one thing one moment and something else the next.

A messaging screen that doesn't make full use of the touchscreen

Editing on the iOS Messages screen still means an Edit button in the top left that you have to tap first. Tapping a message only opens its details, and a long press does nothing.

This "Edit button" pattern is everywhere in iOS, like the alarm editing mentioned above. It's very different from Android, where a long press generally means editing the item you pressed. iOS doesn't assign any action to a long press, which adds yet another step. It really doesn't make full use of the interaction advantages of the touchscreen itself.

The soy sauce bottle in the kitchen

There's a soy sauce brand called Haitian with an incredibly annoying seal design. You open the cap, pull the ring tab, pour out the rich soy sauce, and then you discover the cap won't close anymore! Soy sauce is something you use over a long time; I have no idea what a one-time design like a soda-can pull tab is for.

Compare that with another condiment bottle in the kitchen, the white vinegar, and the gap in design is obvious. The vinegar has a big cap that's easy to twist open, and to help control the flow when pouring, there's a narrow slit inside that regulates it. Convenient in the extreme.

entry.title: Reading Notes on JavaScript: The Definitive Guide (6th Edition, the Rhino Book)
entry.content:
Notes from reading JavaScript: The Definitive Guide, on the parts I consider core or easy to get confused about.
I'll also add some good articles I read along the way that expand on them.

Changelog

2016-01-18 Updated up to the try-except-finally statement
2016-04-07 Renamed the post. Split its structure into core parts and fuzzy points

What I consider the core of the book

  1. The core of the language
  2. Variable types
  3. Strict mode
  4. Lexical scope, functions, closures, this, call, apply, bind
  5. The prototype system

Core parts

The language core

Variables and their types

Variables in JavaScript have no type of their own. When you assign a value to a variable, the variable is really just referencing that value. This is the same as in Python.

Both differ from fixed-type variables in languages like C. In C, when you declare a variable you have to specify its type, and the variable is actually a fixed-size chunk of space that holds the value directly. Arrays are the same: an array can only store values of a single type, and C decides how much memory to allocate based on the type, for example 4 bytes for an int.

In JavaScript and Python you don't declare a variable's type. A variable is just a reference to data, and the type is determined by the data itself: whatever type of value the variable references, that's the variable's type. Data types in JavaScript fall into two groups (apparently borrowed from Java):

Primitive types

  • Primitive types (5 of them)
    • Numbers
    • Strings
    • Booleans
    • null
    • undefined

Note: primitives are not objects, but you may have seen calls of the form APrimitiveType.method. That's because numbers, strings and booleans have the concept of "wrapper objects".

Object types

  • Object types (object) (every data type other than the 5 primitives is an object type)
    • Plain objects (name-value pairs)
    • Arrays
    • Functions - JavaScript can treat function objects like ordinary objects

Strict mode: use strict

If you know a bit of JavaScript history, you'll know Brendan Eich designed it in ten days, drawing mainly on Scheme, Self, C, Java and other languages. Even with existing languages to borrow from, a really rigorous design in that little time wasn't realistic, so JavaScript carried some hidden flaws from the very start. Add the rapid spread during the browser wars, and these flaws never had enough time to be fixed before becoming part of the standard, which is why they have stuck around.

For a quick look at these flaws, see Ruan Yifeng's (a well-known Chinese tech blogger) article Ten design flaws of JavaScript, and the book JavaScript: The Good Parts.

use strict is actually a directive added in ECMAScript 5. It's very close to a statement but differs from one: it contains no keyword, is just a string literal, and can only appear in particular positions.

The purpose of use strict is to make the code after it run in JS's "strict mode", a subset of the language that fixes some important flaws and provides robust error checking and stronger security. Strict and non-strict mode differ in some important ways:

  • The with statement can't be used in strict mode
  • In strict mode every variable must be declared with var first (in non-strict mode, using an undeclared variable adds a new property to the global object)
  • In strict mode, the this value in a function call is undefined rather than the global object.

Fuzzy points

Wrapper objects

Primitives are not objects, but you may have seen calls of the form APrimitiveType.method. That's because numbers, strings and booleans have the concept of "wrapper objects". In other words, when you use the . operator on one of them, JavaScript automatically calls new String(s) | new Number(s) | new Boolean(s) to temporarily convert these three primitive types into objects that inherit the methods of the corresponding type.

// A classic example
var s = "test";
s.len = 4;  // Because of the dot operator, a temporary String object is created here, but it is destroyed right away
var t = s.len; // A String object is created here too, but it is not the one above, hence undefined
  • null and undefined have no wrapper objects
  • You can construct wrapper objects explicitly with the constructors.

Variable hoisting and variable configurability

  • Hoisting
    • A variable declared with var is moved up to the top of the scope it lives in
  • Configurability
    • Global variables are properties of the global object; local variables have no such rule
    • Global variables declared with var are non-configurable and can't be removed with the delete operator

The eval operator

eval() is actually a function, but it has long been treated as an operator. ECMAScript tries to constrain how eval() behaves so that it looks like an expression.

That's because treating eval as an ordinary function without any restrictions has many drawbacks. First, eval() executes code dynamically, which breaks the original code structure and is hard for the interpreter to optimize. Second, if eval were an ordinary function, it could be assigned to another name, say g = eval, so anywhere g is used would have the same problem, making JavaScript code hard to optimize and performance worrying.

In short, if eval behaves like an operator, these serious problems go away. So the ECMAScript grammar keeps constraining it to make it behave more like an operator.

Labeled statements

Mainly used together with continue and break to allow more flexible jumps.

throw/try/catch/finally statements

I wrote an earlier post, Python Pitfalls I Fell Into, which covered an easy trap with try/except/finally in Python.

JavaScript has the same trap. As that post explains, since finally is designed to run no matter what, once a jump statement appears in finally, whatever the other blocks return is ignored.

function finallyTest(){
    var x = 'catch', y = 'except', z = 'finally';
    try {
        k = x + y;
        a = b;
        console.log("here is try------------");
    } catch(e) {
        console.log("here is catch----------");
        return x;
    } finally{
        console.log("here is finally---------");
        return z;
    }
}
// Run
finallyTest()
// Return value
here is catch----------
here is finally---------
'finally'

Function names

// A function declared directly has a function name
function foo(){}
foo.name  // the function name is foo
var bar = foo
bar.name  // assigning a function to a variable just points the variable at the function structure; it does not change the structure itself
// A function expression produces an anonymous function
var foo = function(){}
foo.name // "" (empty string)
// The function name exists only inside the function's own structure, and passing it around does not change that structure
function foo(){}
var o ={
    a: 'a',
    bar: foo
};
o.bar.name // foo

Losing the this reference

// Can happen when a function is passed around several times
function foo(){
    console.log(this.a);
}
var obj = {
    a: 2,
    foo: foo
};
var bar = obj.foo;
var a="oops, global";
bar(); //"oops, global"
// Can happen in callbacks (async)
// same code as above
setTimeout(obj.foo, 100); // "oops, global"

entry.title: Migrating GitLab Data Between Docker Hosts
entry.content:
Where it started: Docker's file-system pit

Our GitLab was deployed with Docker, which was quick and convenient.

Then an application on the server developed a memory leak, and to my surprise, after rebooting the server the whole of Docker was dead. Starting a container kept hitting a series of fairly low-level "filesystem unknown" errors, and the error details came in more than one flavor. After some digging I found that the devicemapper storage driver Docker was using had a bug, and judging from Docker's official GitHub, plenty of people had run into it. The discussion is here: docker fails to mount the block device for the container on devicemapper. It felt like I had fallen into a bottomless pit.

The fix offered on Stack Overflow and GitHub was: stop Docker, delete everything in /var/lib/docker, then restart GitLab. That looked to me like possibly another pit, and I didn't dare jump in. So I chose to study the problem slowly, and in the meantime redeploy GitLab on another server and migrate the data over.

Migrating the GitLab data

I thought the migration would be simple. It turned out there were plenty of pits waiting there too.

First I backed up GitLab's volumes on the original server, copied the backed-up volume files straight to the new server, mounted them the same way as before, and started it up.

Problems I hit

First, Redis complained about not having permission for something or other, so I googled around and fixed the permissions.
Then came an "undefined method" error. It turned out to be caused by the database not having been migrated.

Another hidden pit is the GitLab version. For critical services like this, try not to use latest as the version tag. Otherwise, when something goes wrong you'll have to work out which version you were actually running, and if you can't find out... get ready to rely on pure luck.

The final solution

Jumping into the pits one at a time like this felt pretty dumb, and later I found that someone had already filled them all in: Migrate a Gitlab Docker container from version 8.0.4 to 8.2.0

Appendix: the original guide

The Chinese version of this post includes my full translation of the guide above. For English readers, please read the original directly: Migrate a Gitlab Docker container from version 8.0.4 to 8.2.0. It walks through twelve steps, from stopping the container and backing up the volumes, through fixing the known permission issues and re-running the database migrations, to clearing the Redis cache.

One note of my own on it: step 4, removing the GitLab container, is optional if you are moving the data to a Docker GitLab instance on a different server.

entry.title: Analyzing Concepts in Computer Science
entry.content:
Conceptual analysis?

On "concept," from Wikipedia. To keep the concept complete, I've quoted a fairly long passage here:

A concept, also called an idea, is an abstract, general thought or notion, or an entity that serves as a category or class designating entities, events or relations. Concepts ignore the differences among the things in their extension and treat them as if they were identical, so concepts are abstract. They apply equally to everything in their extension, so they are universal. Concepts are also the basic elements of propositions, just as words are the basic semantic elements of sentences.

Concepts are bearers of meaning, not agents of meaning. A single concept can be expressed in any number of languages; terms are the forms in which concepts are expressed. The concept of a dog can be expressed as Hund in German, chien in French and perro in Spanish. The fact that concepts are, in a sense, independent of language is what makes translation possible: words in different languages have the same meaning because they express the same concept.

A concept is a person's understanding of a complex process or thing. Philosophically speaking, the concept is the basic unit of thought. In everyday usage, people often treat a concept as equivalent to a word or a noun (a term). Chinese culture is traditionally regarded as not emphasizing the definition of concepts, and therefore as not having developed logic and the related philosophy and science.

Conceptual analysis means tracing the meaning, origin and possible contexts of a word. It's extremely common in philosophy: before discussing any question, you first have to analyze every concept in it and get completely clear on what each word means, and only then can the discussion move forward.

Rhetoric and distortion in translation

There are many reasons conceptual analysis is needed. A concept's meaning may have shifted over time, or a word may be entirely foreign and have lost its original meaning in translation. Computer science is itself an imported science in China, and nearly all of its technical terms are translations. So conceptual analysis here leans more toward removing the distortions introduced by translation.

In computer science, none of the many books I've read so far, not even the formal computer science education I received, included anything on analyzing terms. And because Chinese tends to value rhetoric over analysis, images that were fairly plain in the original English may, once translated into Chinese, pick up implicit rhetorical devices for the sake of elegance or imagery, and start to become mysterious. At that point, going back to the original word becomes very important.

Some such translations:

  • handle, translated as 句柄 (literally "phrase handle")
  • socket, translated as 套接字 (literally "sleeve-joint word")
  • meta-programming, translated as 元编程 (literally "primal programming")
    and so on. In English these meanings are fairly plain, but in Chinese, to keep the terms concise and elegant, the translators borrowed a lot of native imagery, and that imagery is itself rather hazy. The originally clear meaning becomes hazy and hard to grasp. These translations are products of their history and the technical background of their time. If they were made today, they probably wouldn't be done that way at all; the key words might even be kept in English.

When we run into such words, we need to look at when they were translated and what the source word was before it became Chinese. Once we find the source word, we should understand it within its own context. But even the source word deserves analysis, because it didn't come out of nowhere either. Computing is a very young science, and many of its words are newly coined. Some were made up outright; others also used some rhetoric, extending an original meaning into the computing domain.

A word isn't extended without reason. Behind it there's usually some inner connection between concepts, and this often forms a rhetorical device: metaphor.

The metaphors behind concepts

Another benefit of conceptual analysis is that it lets us see the metaphors behind concepts, which in turn helps us understand a concept's core idea better and more deeply.

For example, a few metaphors I personally like:

  • docker: the dockworker metaphor
  • handle: the door-handle metaphor
  • callback: the call-you-back metaphor
  • hook: the hook metaphor

What these metaphors have in common is that their plain original meaning is connected, in a somewhat implicit way, to the concept in computer science: the two share a very similar structure or meaning. If you want to grasp what a term means quickly, it's very important to combine its metaphor with the context at hand.

The philosophy behind conceptual analysis

Distinguishing the "efficient cause" from the "final cause"

To be continued

entry.title: Iterators and Generators in Python
entry.content:
Just a quick write-up, since producing something is a better test of how well you understand it. Also, I feel a lot of articles online aren't very reliable. Quite obviously their authors haven't even read the official documentation and just write summaries from experience, which can easily mislead people.

Iterator Types

First, the part on iteration in the official Python 2.7 documentation

The passages below are quoted from the official documentation, Iterator Types. Before reading, it helps to be clear on what a few words mean:

  • "iterator"
  • "iteration"
  • "iterable"
  • "container": an object that can hold other objects, such as a list or a dictionary

New in version 2.2.
Python supports a concept of iteration over containers. This is implemented using two distinct methods; these are used to allow user-defined classes to support iteration. Sequences, described below in more detail, always support the iteration methods.

One method needs to be defined for container objects to provide iteration support:
container.__iter__()
Return an iterator object. The object is required to support the iterator protocol described below. If a container supports different types of iteration, additional methods can be provided to specifically request iterators for those iteration types. (An example of an object supporting multiple forms of iteration would be a tree structure which supports both breadth-first and depth-first traversal.) This method corresponds to the tp_iter slot of the type structure for Python objects in the Python/C API.

The iterator objects themselves are required to support the following two methods, which together form the iterator protocol:

iterator.__iter__()
Return the iterator object itself. This is required to allow both containers and iterators to be used with the for and in statements. This method corresponds to the tp_iter slot of the type structure for Python objects in the Python/C API.

iterator.next()
Return the next item from the container. If there are no further items, raise the StopIteration exception. This method corresponds to the tp_iternext slot of the type structure for Python objects in the Python/C API.
Python defines several iterator objects to support iteration over general and specific sequence types, dictionaries, and other more specialized forms. The specific types are not important beyond their implementation of the iterator protocol.
The intention of the protocol is that once an iterator’s next() method raises StopIteration, it will continue to do so on subsequent calls. Implementations that do not obey this property are deemed broken. (This constraint was added in Python 2.3; in Python 2.2, various iterators are broken according to this rule.)

Sorting out the concepts

That's roughly the core of what Python 2.7 says about iteration. To sum it up:

For a container object to support iteration, it needs to implement an __iter__() method. This method returns an "iterator object" (iterator). If a container implements this method, we call the container "iterable".

An iterator also needs an __iter__() method, which returns the iterator itself, plus a next() method that returns the next item. An iterator is, of course, itself "iterable". Together, these two methods of an iterator are called the "iterator protocol".

In for and in statements, whether you use a container object (such as a list) or an iterator object, it has to support the __iter__() method. For a container, this method returns an iterator; for an iterator, it returns itself. That is then used for the iteration. In other words, even a container object is first turned into an iterator object before it's iterated over. Python's documentation says so too, in The for statement:

The for statement

The for statement is used to iterate over the elements of a sequence (such as a string, tuple or list) or other iterable object:

for_stmt ::=  "for" target_list "in" expression_list ":" suite ["else" ":" suite]

The expression list is evaluated once; it should yield an iterable object. An iterator is created for the result of the expression_list. The suite is then executed once for each item provided by the iterator, in the order of ascending indices. Each item in turn is assigned to the target list using the standard rules for assignments, and then the suite is executed. When the items are exhausted (which is immediately when the sequence is empty), the suite in the else clause, if present, is executed, and the loop terminates.

Generator Types

The official documentation's definition

From Generator Types:

Python’s generators provide a convenient way to implement the iterator protocol. If a container object’s __iter__() method is implemented as a generator, it will automatically return an iterator object (technically, a generator object) supplying the __iter__() and next() methods. More information about generators can be found in the documentation for the yield expression.

Sorting out the concepts

What this means is that a generator object is just a shortcut for implementing the iterator protocol. Normally, when we need a custom iterator, we have to implement the required __iter__() and next() methods by hand; with a generator object, you automatically get back an iterator that supports the iteration protocol. And to create a generator, all you need is to use a yield expression in a function. That creates a generator function, and when it's called, it returns an iterator (usually called a generator) that controls the execution of the generator function.

From Yield expressions:

The yield expression is only used when defining a generator function, and can only be used in the body of a function definition. Using a yield expression in a function definition is sufficient to cause that definition to create a generator function instead of a normal function.

When a generator function is called, it returns an iterator known as a generator. That generator then controls the execution of a generator function. The execution starts when one of the generator’s methods is called. At that time, the execution proceeds to the first yield expression, where it is suspended again, returning the value of expression_list to generator’s caller. By suspended we mean that all local state is retained, including the current bindings of local variables, the instruction pointer, and the internal evaluation stack. When the execution is resumed by calling one of the generator’s methods, the function can proceed exactly as if the yield expression was just another external call. The value of the yield expression after resuming depends on the method which resumed the execution.

All of this makes generator functions quite similar to coroutines; they yield multiple times, they have more than one entry point and their execution can be suspended. The only difference is that a generator function cannot control where should the execution continue after it yields; the control is always transferred to the generator’s caller

entry.title: The Kuaibo Case and the Standing of Technological Neutrality
entry.content:
This post discusses only the question of "technological neutrality" in the Kuaibo case (Kuaibo was a Chinese video player whose executives were tried in 2016 for spreading pornography; their defense argued that "technology itself is innocent"), and the theory's standing and current state in the philosophy of science.

technological neutrality
Its core claim is that technology is pure and value-neutral, and has in itself no properties of right or wrong, good or evil; technology ends up in human use, and the results it finally produces should be borne by humans themselves.

Technological Neutrality in the Kuaibo Case

The debate in the recent Kuaibo case, as far as the value of technology goes, can be called a microcosm of the discussion technological neutrality has received in the philosophy of science: technological neutrality has persisted in the philosophy of science for a very long time, and it still has a large following today. Among the general public, technological neutrality is even the only value view of technology there is.

Within the value view of technological neutrality, there are some very common arguments:

  • An example from daily life: if someone kills a person with a knife, the guilty party is the person, not the knife, and not the factory that made the knife.
  • An example from science: the atomic bomb is innocent; the guilty are the people who misuse it.
  • An example from the internet: trojans are innocent; the guilty are the people who use them for illegal activities.

These claims all argue for the value-neutral character of technology. I'll explain later where the holes in these arguments are.

Technological Neutrality in the Philosophy of Science

In fact, the view of technological neutrality appeared very early in the philosophy of science, and because of technology's own "self-concealing nature", the values attached to technology naturally tend toward neutrality. After the Industrial Revolution, the ills of technology gradually came to light, and reflection on the value of technology also made new progress in the philosophy of science.

The Premise for Discussing the Value of Technology: When We Discuss the Value of Technology, What Are We Discussing?

"Technology has no value bias. The consequences of any use of technology should, in the final analysis, be borne by humans, whether they are good or bad." Fundamentally, this statement is right, because without humans there would be no technology at all, and so no side effects brought by technology. In this sense, saying "all guilt ultimately falls on humans" is beyond reproach.

But in reality, we can't discuss the problem this way. Even in the philosophy of technology, discussion in the above sense is meaningless; it gives no substantive help to human understanding of technology.

The premise for discussing the value of technology is:

"Technology is created by humans and used by humans. Technology is not 'dead'; it has effects on humans."

Under this premise, when we discuss the value of technology, what we are discussing is: whether technology itself is really pure, and whether technology produces side effects on humans in certain respects. More precisely, technology is created by humans, so does this creation affect humans' construction of themselves?

The Intentional Structure of Technology

Imagine the following scenario:

There are two peoples. One gives its members knives and horses when they are very young. The other gives them poetry and books. What happens when these two peoples grow up? You can imagine that for the first people, the knife becomes their preferred way of speaking. For the second, poetry and books become their chosen way of speaking.

To take an example closer to daily life: once my boss asked me whether using a Mac felt great, and whether using a Mac, using these better tools, just makes you want to write things, makes you want to write code? Use a Mac and you want to write code; use Windows and you want to play games.

The examples above are meant to show that technology has its own intentional structure, and this intentional structure carries an attached value that unconsciously produces side effects on humans. The production of these side effects is not something humans can choose, especially in groups. Living inside their own paradigm, humans lack the ability to clearly discern the long-term effects of an intentional structure.

Note that this only says technology has its own intentional structure that in turn produces unconscious side effects on humans. It makes no value judgment about that intentional structure; that is, it does not judge whether it is good or bad. In fact, that is a very difficult task, and most of the time an impossible one.

On the other hand, saying technology has side effects on humans' construction of themselves is also unlike "determinism" in traditional philosophy, which leads to a situation where humans have no free will, and for any decision they make and any mistake they commit, they need not, and cannot, bear the consequences.

In the philosophy of technology, the thesis of technological non-neutrality holds that "technology and humans construct each other".

Back to the Technological Neutrality Argument in the Kuaibo Case

The intentional structure of technology means it will inevitably produce side effects on humans, and it also exposes a very large hole in the arguments listed earlier: they assume a premise, namely that humans can judge with complete clarity what potential side effects the use of a technology will have. In other words, that humans can clearly know, and control, the counter-effects brought by technology, including both the very obvious ones and the latent ones.

But this is unrealistic. The side effects of many technologies are hard to detect. It's hard for you to know clearly what effect long-term use of WeChat, as a technology, will have, or already has had, on you. Not to mention that humans live inside a great net woven from technologies.

Another aspect is that the side effects technology produces on groups are more complex than those it produces on individuals, because the behavior of a group is not a simple sum of individual behaviors, and the influence a technology has on a group runs deeper. Take programming languages: pure C programmers and Python programmers are bound to differ, and when these differences show up at the group level, they basically reflect the differences in the design philosophies of C and Python, that is, the differences in their own intentional structures.

In other words, the effect a technology produces within a group will end up closer to the technology's own intentional structure: if Kuaibo makes it easy to spread pornographic material, then under natural conditions at the current stage of civilization, it will inevitably spread pornographic material, not study material. Once you understand this, you can see clearly where the key lies: control, regulation, critique, reflection.

This is also what critical theory of technology holds:

"Even though technology has its own intentional structure, what this teaches us is to handle it more cautiously and more critically, rather than directly making a value judgment that affirms or negates it."

Philosophy of Science and Sociotechnical Decision-Making

To be continued

Appendix

I had never thought deeply about the philosophy of technology before. Only from the book Amusing Ourselves to Death did I sense that the relationship between technology and humans isn't as simple as splitting into two. Later I also thought about the problem of technological neutrality, and always felt something was wrong with it but couldn't put my finger on it, until I read Professor Wu Guosheng's Lectures on the Philosophy of Technology and got the answer I'm most satisfied with so far:

"Technology and humans construct each other."

Notes on the Key Points of Lectures on the Philosophy of Technology:

The Humanistic Essence of Technology

  • What is technology?

    • Technology is a way of human existence; technology and humans are not split into two

  • What is the essence of humans?

    • Humans are animals without an essence; the human essence is self-constructed

  • Characteristics of technology

    • Technology is self-concealing, and the history of Western scholarship is a history that values only internal lines of reasoning
    • The problem with technological neutrality: technology has an intentional structure and contains particular value orientations
    • Technology is a link in constructing humans and the world: bodily techniques, humans are all born premature, shaping of the body, shaping of perception. The use of PPT.

Technology and Politics

  • Does technology have politics?

    • Technology and politics are related. Politics intervenes in technology, and technology affects politics: gunpowder wiped out the knightly class and was the gravedigger of the feudal system. Hydraulic societies and centralized power.

  • The political critique of technology

    • The hand mill gave rise to the feudal system; the steam mill gave rise to the capitalist system.

  • Taylorism and Fordism

    • Technology leads to the retreat of human nature: seeing deaths in the news and gradually becoming indifferent

  • Three views of technology

    • Technological optimism: technological neutralists; problems brought by technology can only be solved by technology
    • Technological pessimism: technological autonomy, technology has an internal logic of development; holds that modern society has entered a one-dimensional society, the sense of difference disappears, and the tentacles of technology reach into every field. But it views technology holistically, treating it as monolithic, without working out the various possibilities of technology. Only by going into the details can one get out of pessimism.
    • Critical theory of technology: go into the details of technology and examine every aspect: the theory of technological transformation. Assembly lines, computers, communications, transportation, propaganda technology. For every new technology, ask who benefits and who loses.

Technology and Philosophy

  • The historical absence of the philosophy of technology

    • Beauty, justice, goodness, art and science are all focuses of philosophy; technology is not.
    • Technology itself: its self-concealing nature, and long-standing technological neutrality
    • Philosophy: philosophy emphasizes reasoning and internal logic: essentialism

  • The rise of the philosophy of technology

    • Changes in technology itself: problems with technology have recently appeared; it is no longer transparent
    • Philosophy: the collapse of essentialism and the emergence of phenomenalism. Empiricism inherits nominalism.

entry.title: Python Pitfalls I Fell Into: Import Paths, try/finally, and Dict Comprehensions
entry.content:
Past experience, if not forgotten, is a guide for the future. (前事不忘，后事之师) — Strategies of the Warring States, "Strategies of Zhao I"

Module Imports in Python

Package Imports

This one is fairly simple, so a single example will do. Still, it did trip me up when I was starting out…

# File structure:
packages
├── __init__.py
└── my_module.py
# This is a package import
import packages
# What follows is obtained from attributes defined in __init__.py
packages.some_module.some_method
# This treats the package as one step on the search path
from packages import some_module
some_module.some_method

The Module Search Path

Consider the following scenario:

# Django has a common app, and it has been added to the installed apps list
# File structure of the common app
common
├── __init__.py
├── common.py
├── others.py
└── somethings.py
# somethings.py contains this import statement
from common.others import some_func   # raises an error

In the code above, because the names are the same and the search path by default starts from the directory of the code currently being executed, the common file is found before the common package, so it shadows the package on the search path. Once common is found, Python looks for some_func in the common file, can't find it, and raises an error.

Execution Order in try-except-finally

In Python exception handling, the finally clause is always executed, whether or not an exception is raised in the try clause. Because of this, finally is often used for cleanup, such as closing files or database connections.

If an exception occurs in try-except-finally and is not properly handled, Python first stashes the exception, and after the actions in finally have finished, it passes the stashed exception up to the caller. This execution order is what creates some potential traps.

Look at this example:

def finallyTest():
    print 'start------'
    while  True:
        try:
            print "running------"
            raise IndexError("r")   # raise an IndexError
        except NameError as e:
            print 'NameError happended {0}'.format(str(e))
            break
        finally:
            print 'finally executed'
            break # there is a break statement in finally
            
# run the test function
FinallyTest()
# output:
start------
running------
finally executed

In this example, the try clause raises an IndexError, and the except clause doesn't catch it. You would normally expect the error to propagate up to the caller (here, to the interpreter) and trigger an IndexError. But after the whole function runs, no exception appears.

The reason is that when an exception occurs in the try block and no matching handler is found in the except clauses, the exception is "stashed temporarily." When finally finishes, the stashed exception is "raised again." But if finally raises a new exception or executes a return or break statement, the stashed exception is lost, which leads to "exception masking."

Another, slightly more complicated example:

import logging
logger = logging.Logger(__name__)
def returnTest(a):
    try:
        if a == False:
            raise ValueError("data can not be False")
        else:
            return a  
    except ValueError as e:
        logger.exception("exception!, {detail}").fomat(detail)
        return "return exception in except statement" 
    finally:
        return "return in finally statement"
print returnTest(False)
print returnTest(True)

You would normally expect the first print to trigger the error, enter the except clause and log the exception, and since the statements in finally always run, it returns 'return in finally statement'. The second should return True. In fact, both return 'return in finally statement'.

The reason is the same as in the previous example. Whether in the try suite or the except suite, a return or break, any statement that makes the program jump, is saved first. Then the statements in finally are executed, and as soon as finally contains a jump statement, the program jumps right away, so the saved state above simply disappears.

The Limits of Dict Comprehensions

On one project I ran into an operation that had to query the database many times. Specifically, there were companies, each with attributes such as a name and a company code. Fetching company information from the database every time caused performance problems, so I decided to cache it in a dictionary and wanted to use a dict comprehension. I found that each iteration of a comprehension can only produce a single entry. I had never noticed this before, so I'm writing it down here.

# This works
>>>{model.key: model.value for Modle in models }
# The result is an ordinary dictionary
>>>{key1: value1, key2: value2, ...}
# But using it like this is not supported
>>>{model.key1: model.value1, moedel.key2: model.value2 for model in models}
# The workaround is to make the value above a dictionary, or to use a list comprehension and wrap it in one more list
>>>{model.key1: {models.key1: models.value1, model.key2: model.value2, ...} for model in models}

Here is the real example. The branch-related parts are branch company information, and the subbranch-related parts are sub-branch company information. The goal is to build a dictionary whose keys are branch company names and whose values are the branch's primary key, its number, and the sub-branches under it. The sub-branches are themselves a dictionary, keyed by sub-branch name with the sub-branch's other information as values. Together this forms a two-level dictionary cache of company data.

companys_by_name = {
        branch.name: {
            "pk": branch.pk,
            "number": branch.number,
            "subbranch": {
                subbranch.name: {"pk":subbranch.pk, "number":subbranch.number} for subbranch in SubbranchCompany.objects.filter(branch_company=branch)
            } for branch in BranchCompany.objects.all()
}
# In detail, the meaning is as follows; sub-branches are companies under a branch
company_info_dict = {
     branch_name:{
        "primary key": primary key of the current branch,
        "company number": company number of the current branch,
        "sub-branches":{
            sub_branch_name:{
                "primary key": primary key of the current sub-branch,
                "sub-branch number": number of the current sub-branch,
            } for sub_branch in sub-branches under the current branch
        }
     } for branch in all branches
}

entry.title: Open Questions
entry.content:
