This post is a place to collect questions I run into day to day.
For some of them I have a few preliminary thoughts, which may have big flaws or even be fundamentally wrong. Others I've only just run into or only just thought of, and since I'm inside my own paradigm, I can't yet even tell whether they're naive, or whether the questions themselves are flawed.

Maybe because I've had a little education in the philosophy of science, I always try, while learning something, to understand its final cause. In natural science research, pursuing efficient causes is the best way to grow knowledge, while pursuing final causes often causes problems and isn't realistic. But in computer science, a great many things are defined directly by humans; you could say most of the computing world is something humans created themselves. In that situation, pursuing final causes is the best and deepest way to grow knowledge.

Anyway, I've written down the questions and my current thinking.
For me, the moment I can ask a question is the moment I really start to understand.

Engineering questions

  • What is the relationship between RESTful and ROA (resource-oriented architecture)?
    • I roughly understand RESTful and have done some simple work with it.
    • Taken literally, resource-oriented architecture is an architecture centered on resources. On the backend, for example, you split things up by resource type and then combine fairly independent resources to produce the content you want.
    • As a metaphor, it's like constructing a building where all the raw materials (resources) are supplied in finely divided form, and in theory you can use them to build most kinds of building structures.

Meta questions

  • How learning computer science differs from learning natural science.
    • This is mainly about methodology. In natural science, in physics for example, we might try to find the final cause of something, such as why the speed of light is finite, or, in biology, why ethanol isn't toxic to humans while methanol, with a similar structure, is highly toxic. In natural science research we go straight to finding out how something behaves; this is called the efficient cause, and this approach easily grows knowledge in natural science.
    • In computer science, most of the world is created by humans. Humans directly defined and built this world, so much of the time we can ask about final causes. Even if, in the end, some questions lead back to natural science or the formal sciences, pursuing final causes lets us get to the essence of a problem faster.

entry.title: My Front-End Notes: Understanding HTML
entry.content:
I've dabbled in front-end work before, but every time I ended up touching small details: some HTML element here, what some CSS property means there, or writing a bit of JavaScript and the like. I always felt I lacked a higher-level understanding of the front end.

I'd occasionally hear metaphors about the three pillars of the web page: HTML is the skeleton, responsible for the page's structure; CSS is the skin, responsible for how the page looks; JavaScript is the muscle, powering the page's interactions. But that kind of description seems too broad to give you a concrete understanding.

So this post tries to lay out something between that metaphor and the low-level details. By describing the core role of HTML, CSS, and JavaScript in turn, I want to see whether I can get that bird's-eye view.

First, let's distinguish two front-end concepts: "typesetting" and "layout."

See two answers on Zhihu (a Chinese Q&A site): Typesetting and layout are two different things and Layout and typesetting are different

"Layout" refers to the macro-level division of the GUI, for example when you have several large blocks and want to arrange them in a specified way.

"Typesetting" refers to things like this: you have some paragraphs containing different fonts and font sizes, and you align them to different baselines, wrap lines, break words, and handle overflow sensibly.

Starting from the web page

A web page is the networked aggregate of all kinds of real-world information carriers

The web page is the most direct visible part of the front end. Its purpose is to "present information," and everything else serves that purpose. A web page isn't fundamentally different from any other carrier of information. Think of the information carriers we see in daily life: a Word document, a PDF, a questionnaire, a financial statement, and so on. A web page is a networked aggregate version of these carriers.

When humans look at a web page, what are they looking at?

Just as we treat the information carriers in our lives and the information they hold, we treat web pages in a similar way: first we pay attention to the content the document presents. If the content is formatted beautifully, we may enjoy reading it more and be more willing to read further. And if the carrier has a bit more interactivity, it's even more engaging.

In other words, when humans look at a web page, the order is still content -> style, interaction. Of course, as web pages grow richer and more colorful, style and interaction get more and more weight, to the point of being as important as the content.

Content corresponds to HTML; style and interaction are determined jointly by CSS and JavaScript.

HTML: a semantic document flow

The "two semantics" of a web page

Of course, as an information carrier a web page differs from physical objects in everyday life. Although the ultimate audience for the information on a web page is human, it reaches them through browsers, search engines, or other programs that can process web pages. This gives rise to two kinds of semantics on a web page:

The first is the meaning that is ultimately presented, understood by humans; this is semantics in the everyday sense.
The second is understandable by machine programs such as browsers and search engines; it is "machine-readable semantics."
The semantics ultimately presented are determined by human knowledge structures: humans interpret different content on a page as elements with specific meanings, such as "title," "body," "footnote," and "navigation." This is exactly why some HTML elements come with certain styles built in. Headings h1 through h6, for example, have a larger font size and are bold. That matches human common sense and fits the meaning to be presented, so this default is very convenient.

The second kind, machine-readable semantics, in the sense above, serves the first kind. Browsers, search engines, and other programs recognize the semantic elements in HTML code, then add styles and so on to present the final result. The more semantic the HTML, the easier it is for machines to understand. In software, semantics is usually built on sensible "structuring." Structuring means distinguishing content with different meanings by giving it different structures, and in HTML that structuring is done with the various HTML tags.

Presenting the first kind of semantics in a friendlier way is the overall goal of a web page. That takes close collaboration among designers, information architects, and programmers.

Making the second kind of semantics serve the first kind better is the essential work of the programmer.

Why the second kind of semantics matters

There's a very apt example of why the second kind of semantics matters. I don't know if you've run into this on your smartphone:

When you need to type something on a website, a keyboard pops up. But different input fields bring up different keyboard layouts: when you type an email address you get a keyboard with the @ symbol, when you type a password you get the full keyboard, and so on. Stranger still, this sometimes works and sometimes doesn't. When it works, typing feels very smooth. When it doesn't, you have to switch keyboard layouts by hand to find the symbol you need, which is really annoying.

Behind this is the second kind of semantics at work: in HTML there are many different types of input fields, some email, some password, some text. If a website distinguishes these meanings well and uses them in its HTML, the keyboard pop-up behaves very intelligently, because the machine can choose which layout to show based on the different semantics in the HTML. If it's email, it shows the layout with @; if it's a password, the full keyboard; and so on. Sites with poor semantics can't do this. They just show the generic layout, and the human has to figure it out and switch.

This example shows that as browsers and other software get smarter, semantic HTML becomes more and more important.

As mentioned above, browsers generally give certain HTML elements certain styles, but only because that matches human common sense and is convenient. Never use an element because you want a certain style; instead, choose the element whose meaning best fits the content you're marking up. Styling should be left to CSS. This is also why people sum it up as: "HTML cares only about semantics, not layout, and not style or interaction."

Understanding a web page through HTML semantics

Having covered why semantics matters, let's look at how to understand a web page through these elements of the second kind. Quite a few elements are involved here, so this is only a rough outline.

First, web pages have quite a few semantic elements for presenting information.

The most basic ones, like

<!--header-->
<header></header>
<!--main body-->
<main></main>
<!--footer-->
<footer></footer>
<!--paragraph-->
<p></p>
<!--section-->
<section></section>
<!--self-contained piece-->
<artical></artical>
...

and more specific ones:

<!--time-->
<time></time>
<!--address-->
<address></address>
...

These are all ordinary semantic elements for presenting information. But just as in real life, there are other ways to present information that help humans read and understand it better. For example:

  • Lists
    They lay out the core information point by point and category by category, letting people quickly grasp the key aspects of something. In HTML

  • Embedded elements
    Such as images; a picture is worth a thousand words.
    And music, video, and so on

Also, in real life we often hand out paper forms to collect information, and use reports to clearly present information sorted into categories in a fairly structured format. HTML has corresponding semantic elements for these:

  • Forms (form)
  • Tables (table)

They serve much the same purpose as their real-life counterparts. HTML forms come in many types: radio buttons, checkboxes, input fields (and input fields themselves have finer-grained semantic types). That mirrors the many kinds of surveys and forms in real life.

HTML also has some semantic elements of its own. For example:

<!--link, perhaps the most important unique element: it ties pages together over the network-->
<a></a>
<!--some other elements, which describe relationships between pages, page information, and so on-->
<link>
<meta>

Those are basically the kinds of HTML elements there are. Combined, they include parts for collecting information and parts for presenting it, and to present information better, HTML provides many semantic elements.

Put together, these elements form all the semantic information of a web page. They can implement and imitate almost every real-world information carrier, and in some respects even surpass them.

The document flow

Besides the elements mentioned earlier that carry some styles based on common sense (if those count as typesetting styles), HTML also has a simple default way of laying things out (let's call it layout style): elements are arranged in order from top to bottom and left to right. To put it more vividly, this is called the HTML document flow.

This default document flow gives HTML a common-sense, most basic layout, so that elements don't all end up heaped together in a mess. But I'll stress it again: although browsers give HTML some default styles and layout, these are all based on human intuition and common sense: "HTML cares only about semantics, not layout, and not style or interaction."

DOM

DOM stands for Document Object Module, that is, the Document Object Model. Here is the explanation from W3.org:

What is the Document Object Model?

The Document Object Model is a platform- and language-neutral interface that will allow programs and scripts to dynamically access and update the content, structure and style of documents. The document can be further processed and the results of that processing can be incorporated back into the presented page.

Why the Document Object Model?

“Dynamic HTML” is a term used by some vendors to describe the combination of HTML, style sheets and scripts that allows documents to be animated. The W3C has received several submissions from members companies on the way in which the object model of HTML documents should be exposed to scripts. These submissions do not propose any new HTML tags or style sheet technology. The W3C DOM Activity is working hard to make sure interoperable and scripting-language neutral solutions are agreed upon.

What are those two paragraphs saying?

In other words, the DOM is the Document Object Model. It isn't part of some specific language's standard library or anything like that; it's a model independent of language and platform. Any other language that wants to manipulate HTML documents (actually not just HTML, but also XML and some other structured languages) has to design its way of doing so according to this object model.

The reason the DOM came about is that a bunch of people used to be at each other's throats: you had your ideas, I had mine. To unify the martial world, the W3C proposed the DOM and has kept standardizing it, which is good for everyone.

The DOM itself is a fairly complex thing, but for the DOM we use day to day, it's enough to know roughly what it looks like and how to manipulate it to count as getting started. When we talk about the DOM, we really mean a tree structure of HTML:

With the tree structure in the figure above, other languages that implement DOM manipulation, such as JavaScript, can operate on these nodes according to certain rules. The DOM tree itself also defines some concepts of inheritance, which make it easier to control its nodes.

Summary

That's basically the whole core of HTML. To sum it up in a few words: semantics, common-sense default styles for elements, the document flow, and the DOM.

entry.title: The Three-Body Problem, The Walking Dead, and Social Darwinism
entry.content:
It has been several years since I read Big Liu's (Liu Cixin's, as fans call him) The Three-Body Problem. Apart from the grand narrative and a few classic scenes, I've forgotten most of it. When I started watching The Walking Dead, I took it for a straightforward zombie show, but as the plot went deeper I found it was describing a lot more. In some important respects, such as the setup of the world, the two are very similar. One extends Darwinism to the whole universe and builds a rather extreme, Darwinian cosmic sociology. The other drops humanity into a world full of death, where small groups survive dark-forest style, reshuffling a world order that took millions of years to form since humans first appeared and taking a fresh look at humans as a species. It too is steeped in Darwinian thought.

The basic setups of The Three-Body Problem and The Walking Dead

Both setups are heavily Darwinian and put great weight on the struggle for survival.

The basis of the theory of evolution

In a given environment, resources are limited and can support only a certain number of living things, while the number of living things keeps growing. To win the limited resources they need, they must struggle to survive: the winners live on and the losers are eliminated.

The setup of The Three-Body Problem

Big Liu extends this idea to the whole universe and sets up a similar sociology at the cosmic scale: the universe's total resources are also limited, all kinds of civilizations live in it, and the more advanced a civilization, the more resources it needs. At the same time, every civilization's highest principle is that "survival is the primary need of a civilization"; it wants to survive. In such a universe, Big Liu plays out civilizations' strategies for survival.

The setup of The Walking Dead

A sudden virus disrupts the existing world order and drops the surviving humans into a world of walkers, full of danger on every side and short of the resources needed to live, to show how humans survive at the end of the world.

Strategies in The Three-Body Problem and The Walking Dead

The Three-Body Problem

Whether it's the Trisolarans' interference by sophons or the Singer's erasure by dual-vector foil, the strategy is pure dark forest: no cooperation, no game playing. "I destroy you, and what does that have to do with you?" Blunt and direct. You could say it pushes the struggle for survival to its limit. The loser mentality mocked in "Trust in Losers and Never Be Redeemed" [1], the review that has long held the top spot in the Three-Body section of Douban (a Chinese book and film review site), is exactly this survival-competition thinking pushed to the extreme.

The Walking Dead

It adds more elements. The protagonist's job before the apocalypse was police officer: the best representative of the old world order and its rules. It also examines humanity and morality: police officers, soldiers, doctors, teachers, priests, ordinary citizens, children and others each stand for a different kind of person and are shown in different ways. Survival strategies of every kind, family-style, community-style, trap-style, are examined one by one.

Order in The Three-Body Problem and The Walking Dead

The Three-Body Problem

The whole story opens against the backdrop of the Cultural Revolution, and what it sets out to highlight is the tense atmosphere of suspicion of that period and the chaos of moral order at the time: a single political movement was enough to incite countless people to push the so-called morality and humanity of thousands of years of civilization into the abyss. One major theme of the Cultural Revolution was how to survive, and that was only within humanity itself. Extend these fragile things to different civilizations across the whole universe and magnify them, and the dark forest is not unimaginable. Losing reason can overturn morality and humanity, and so can complete reason. Big Liu shows one such possible cruelty: morality and the like are too unreliable, and what can be relied on are strict rules of the game. The Swordholder logic understands the rules; Cheng Xin (in my view the "saintly" Cheng Xin is the spokesperson for morality and humanity) doesn't understand them, or rather doesn't want to. "Lose humanity, and you lose much; lose bestiality, and you lose everything." Big Liu stresses this point in different ways [2].

The Walking Dead

It keeps the story on Earth and clearly examines different kinds of people in much more detail and in many different ways. As the plot develops, the conflict between humans and walkers, though always an important backdrop, gradually fades, while conflict between humans and humans comes to the fore. Tens of thousands of years ago humans gradually began forming societies and used language, technology and so on to discipline themselves, eventually more or less completing their own domestication and forming a world of meaning that represses themselves [3]. I think this could be called the technological origin of morality and world order. But this order arose from a particular stage of humanity combined with a particular environment, and the apocalypse ended the old order along with the social and natural conditions that went with it. In the new environment, how should highly evolved modern humans survive? Can they rebuild a different world order? How will moral standards change? After going through many situations, Rick and his group gradually shake off the influence of the old world order. In this group led by a policeman you can still see things beyond survival, and their minds still waver, but the struggle for survival has sunk deeper and deeper into the group's consciousness. I don't know what strategy would serve their survival best, but it will certainly differ from the dark forest of The Three-Body Problem.

Darwinian thought and sociology

Darwin's idea of the struggle for survival holds a significant place in sociology, and a social Darwinism grew out of it. Applying Darwin's ideas to sociology also produces analyses that are logically clear and especially seductive, much like analysis in the sciences (The Three-Body Problem is one such case). But Darwin himself overemphasized the role of the struggle for survival and neglected phenomena beyond it, and when applied to society it struggles to handle complex social phenomena. Besides, Darwin's idea is only "evolution" in the sense of change over time, not "evolution" in the sense of progress.

January 2016, Huilongguan, Beijing

Notes

[1]: For details see "Trust in Losers and Never Be Redeemed" (信卢瑟，永世不得超生). I personally don't agree with this review. What I disagree with is not whether its criticism hits The Three-Body Problem where it hurts. Quite the opposite: the review is right that the book does adopt an extreme, even radical, principle of survival competition. What I disagree with is its misunderstanding of science fiction as a genre. A common technique in science fiction is to assume a premise and then build out a self-consistent world from it. Since Big Liu assumed that survival is the primary need of a civilization, a novel written from that premise is bound to look like this. Of course you could assume that survival is not the primary need of a civilization and describe a relatively harmonious universe, but that would be a different story. A similar example is the classic science-fiction stories built on the premise "what if ice were denser than water". Under such a counterfactual premise, you can't fault the author for the premise itself. What you should look at is whether the world the author shows under that premise is self-consistent, and how deep the portrayal goes.

[2]: In his new book Liu Cixin on Science Fiction, Liu Cixin reveals that he is a scientism believer and a worshipper of technology. The worlds he builds are often as hard and cold as steel, short on humane concern. I think this is a weakness, but also a strength.

[3]: Here I draw on Wu Guosheng's Lectures on the Philosophy of Technology, which gives a lecture-style overview of the philosophy of technology. Human self-discipline is one of its important themes.

entry.title: East and West in the History of Science
entry.content:
I: "Science" in the History of Science

The scope of science studied in the history of science goes beyond what we mean by science in everyday life. The history of science deals with science in a broader sense, which generally includes the following:

  • The rational science of ancient Greece
  • The mathematical-experimental science born of the Scientific Revolution
  • Natural history in a broader sense
  • Science in the widest sense, including technological systems

The main line of the "history of Western science" that the question refers to runs:

  • Ancient Greece
  • Rome
  • The Middle Ages
  • The Renaissance
  • The Scientific Revolution
  • The present

"Science" in what follows is also used in this broad sense, but the main line and the side branches of Western scientific development will be obvious at a glance. One very important thread is the relationship between the type of civilization and the type of science.

II: East and West in the History of Science

If we trace science back to its origins, there are two fairly typical types of science in its history: the "practical science" of the East and the "rational science" of ancient Greece. The civilizations that carried these two types of science also fall into two types: hydraulic civilizations and non-hydraulic civilizations.

Hydraulic Civilizations and Practical Science:

The representatives are the four great ancient civilizations:

  • The Mesopotamian civilization between the Tigris and the Euphrates
  • The Egyptian civilization of the Nile valley
  • The Indian civilization of the Indus and Ganges valleys
  • The Chinese civilization of the Yangtze and Yellow River valleys

All of these civilizations grew up beside water, with people gathering along well-developed river systems to farm. In this kind of civilization, keeping the state running normally and keeping the people fed were the ruling class's first concerns. Accordingly, science, which was held by the ruling class, leaned toward the practical, concentrating on water management (indispensable for irrigation), astronomy (needed for farming, for daily life, and for predicting the fate of the dynasty), and medicine.

Non-Hydraulic Civilization and Greek Rational Science:

Geographically, Greece lies on the Mediterranean coast. The land is mountainous, with no large rivers and no broad, fertile alluvial plains, so irrigation depended more on rain than on river water management. Unable to sustain themselves on local conditions alone, the Greeks gradually developed strong seafaring and trade. At the same time, Greece was neither too close to nor too far from Mesopotamia and Egypt: close enough for exchange, far enough not to be fully assimilated. In addition, the mountains split Greek political life into many small city-states, which both cooperated and competed with one another. In this environment the Greeks developed the democratic city-state and slavery, which guaranteed the emergence of a leisured class, while a free, democratic environment made political debate the norm. All of this cultivated the Greek spirit of reason. Unlike the administrators of the East, who had to strain to keep a centralized empire running, the Greek leisured class paid more attention to thinking about questions such as political legitimacy. These conditions made Greece a remarkable anomaly in the history of science. The Greeks were good at argument, had a passion for getting to the bottom of things, and had a scholarly spirit that rose above worldly concerns. Greek astronomy, for example, differed from the practical astronomy of the East: it was a mathematical planetary astronomy whose aim was to explain nature, not to serve farming, astrology or other practical ends. Explaining nature by nature itself, without appealing to gods or other external agents, and moving from Thales's "water is the origin of all things" to Plato's theory of Forms and on to Aristotle's comprehensive natural philosophy, clearly shows how rational science emerged. This is also the oldest source of modern science.

III: How the Two Types of Science Developed

The Inheritance and Development of Greek Rational Science:

Greece developed a rational scientific tradition that was disinterested, fairly systematic and driven by its own internal logic: Ptolemy's Almagest and Euclid's Elements, for example, and, more importantly, the rational paradigms founded by Plato and Aristotle. Plato's theory of Forms and Aristotle's natural philosophy differ, but both are rational systems with an internal logic. After the fall of Greco-Roman civilization, this rationality was absorbed into Christian doctrine, forming patristic philosophy in the earlier period and scholasticism in the later. Greek culture was at the same time transplanted into the Islamic world, and after the Crusades it began to revive in Europe. After the Age of Discovery, the Reformation and the Renaissance, the main line of Greek rational science was joined up again in Copernicus. Close behind came the Scientific Revolution of the early modern period. Note that this was the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries: capitalism played a role in the development of science, but its influence was nowhere near what it would be during the Industrial Revolution. The main driving force in this period was still the internal logic of rational science, and the religious spirit also gave it a considerable push. (The role of religion in the birth of modern science is also very important, but discussing it would take a great deal of space. The "strict constraints of religion" mentioned in the question are not quite fair.)

The Development of Practical Science in the Hydraulic Civilizations of the East:

Practical science has no internal logic of development. It develops according to the needs of its external environment, and once that environment no longer demands anything, it loses its momentum. This shows very clearly in Chinese history. China is a very typical hydraulic civilization, characterized by centralized politics and officially controlled science. Science driven by external demand of this kind is tied very closely to those demands, and over the long run this shows up as a discontinuous development of science and technology that never forms a system. Moreover, in a highly centralized state like China, once a corresponding culture of statecraft has formed, that culture strongly restricts scholarship that is transcendent and useless. (Whether this is religion or culture is a question in itself.) Over two thousand years of history, China's science and technology (in the sense of technological systems and natural history) was in fact always very strong, reaching its peak in the Ming dynasty. By that point external needs had largely been met. Unless there was a change in social structure (like capitalism and the rise of cities), or science itself developed a structure like Greek rational science, it was hard for science and technology to move further forward. Both were difficult: in the first case, feudal forces kept stifling the sprouts of capitalism; in the second, China's political culture had already set and become a strong constraint. This happened to be exactly when the West picked up the thread of Greek rationality and began its revival, and from then on China began to fall behind in technology as well.

IV: Conclusion

In short, from a Whig-history perspective, the logic of Western scientific development is fairly clear at the macro level. The main line is the Greek thread of rationality; the side branch is the transplanting and re-transplanting of Greek learning by the Islamic world during the Middle Ages. The Islamic world, however, always remained a typical Eastern civilization. Even though it transplanted Greek learning and had an extremely important influence on the birth of modern science, it never managed to become the birthplace of modern science.

Aristotle held that free scholarship requires three conditions:

  • A leisured class
  • A critical tradition
  • Wonder at the world

Looking at the history of science, both ancient Greece and early modern Europe fit these conditions fairly well, while centralized states find them hard to meet. Note that "democracy" is not emphasized here. The point is only that scholarship needs a relatively free environment to develop; once a centralized state has shed its ignorance, it can also create similar conditions.

Huilongguan, Beijing, January 7, 2016

entry.title: Using Raw SQL in Django
entry.content:
The ORM Is Not a Silver Bullet

In terms of features, Django's ORM is only a subset of SQL. That means there are many things SQL can do that the Django ORM can't, not to mention that SQL is even Turing-complete. For example, it wasn't until version 1.8 that Django gradually added control-flow constructs like CASE, WHEN and IF. Yet these are very common in certain kinds of table operations, such as reporting.

Fortunately, Django provides an interface for raw SQL, so you can use raw SQL to implement more complex features.

SQL Control Flow: A CASE WHEN Example

Say we have an archive table, archives:

Fields:

  • number archive number
  • type archive type
  • status archive status
  • company company
  • branch_company branch company

The requirement is to compute, for each type and each branch company, the total number of archives, the number of archives with status=01, and their share of the total.

Of course you could do this in a programming language, but it would be fairly involved. Here you can use a CASE WHEN statement to precisely control which values of the same field get selected.

SELECT 
      COUNT(CASE WHEN status='01' THEN status END) AS status_01,
      COUNT(*) AS total,
      CONCAT(FORMAT(COUNT(CASE WHEN status='01' THEN status END)/
      COUNT(*)*100, 2), '%') AS percentage
FROM
      archives
GROUP BY
      status, branch_company

That solves the problem above. Since this table was made up for the example, I won't show the results here.

Chained Queries on Top of That

One very handy feature of Django's ORM is chained queries: you can keep chaining filter and similar methods to narrow down to exactly what you want.

This is especially useful in certain scenarios. With the table above, for example, sometimes you want data for a particular branch or sub-branch company, and sometimes data for a single type. Writing a separate SQL query for every combination of conditions gets very complicated, and sometimes there are a huge number of combinations. Chained queries solve this problem quite neatly.

To give raw SQL a simple form of chained querying, we need to keep appending condition clauses to the WHERE. A small class does the job:

class GenQuerySQL(object):
    def __init__(self, table):
        self.table = table
        self.group_by_fields = " "
        self.where_conditions = " 1=1 "
        self.fields = " "
        self.order_by_fields = ""
    def where(self, where_condition):
        if where_condition:
            self.where_conditions += " and " + where_condition
        return self
    def add_field(self, fields):
        self.fields += " " + fields
        return self
    def group_by(self, group_by_field):
        self.group_by_fields = group_by_field
        return self
    def order_by(self, order_by_field):
        self.order_by_fields = order_by_field
        return self
    def sql(self):
        SQL = 'SELECT ' + self.fields + ' FROM ' + self.table + ' WHERE ' + self.where_conditions + ' GROUP BY ' + self.group_by_fields + ' ORDER BY ' + self.order_by_fields + ";"
        return SQL

This class gives a simple imitation of chained queries. For example:

archive_statistics = GenQuerySQL('SOME_TABLE')
raw_sql = archive_statistics.add_field('fields').where('where_condition').group_by('group_by_fields').order_by('order_by_fields').sql()

Here .where can be chained multiple times. You could also do it another way: first build the WHERE clause from your conditions, then assemble the final SQL statement. The idea is the same: filter the conditions first, then query the database.

Huilongguan, Beijing, January 2016

entry.title: Deploying GitLab with Docker: Volumes, HTTPS via Nginx, SMTP and SSH
entry.content:
Pulling the Image and Starting the Container

Reference: gitlab documentation

First, pull the Docker image with the dao accelerator:

dao pull gitlab/gitlab-ce

Creating volumes

Simply put, volumes are storage outside the container that can be mapped into it. You can keep fairly generic configuration files, data or code as volumes on the host machine where the container runs. This not only keeps the data permanently and safely, it also makes it easy to change what's in the volumes and map them back into the container, which is very useful for containers whose files need frequent changes.
For this GitLab deployment, I created three volumes: the config, logs and data directories under /mnt/volumes/gitlab.
Start a GitLab container:

sudo docker run --detach \
    --hostname git.xiaohuruwei.com \
    --publish 8443:443 --publish 8080:80 --publish 2222:22 \
    --name gitlab \
    --restart always \
    --volume /mnt/volumes/gitlab/config:/etc/gitlab \
    --volume /mnt/volumes/gitlab/logs:/var/log/gitlab \
    --volume /mnt/volumes/gitlab/data:/var/opt/gitlab \
    gitlab/gitlab-ce:latest

What the options mean:

–hostname
The domain bound inside the container, used when repositories are created. Here it is bound to git.xiaohuruwei.com.

–publish
Port mapping: the part before the colon is the host port, the part after is the port the container exposes.

–volume
Volume mapping: the part before the colon is a path on the host, the part after is the path inside the container.

Configuring Nginx for HTTPS

Reference: gitlab set nginx

Nginx configuration file

server {
    listen 80;
    server_name git.xiaohuruwei.com;
    access_log /var/log/nginx/gitlab.xiaohuruwei.access.log;
    error_log /var/log/nginx/gitlab.xiaohuruwei.error.log;
    rewrite ^ https://git.xiaohuruwei.com;
}

HTTPS proxy

server {
    listen       443 ssl;
    server_name  git.xiaohuruwei.com;
    access_log /var/log/nginx/https-gitlab.xiaohuruwei.access.log;
    error_log /var/log/nginx/https-gitlab.xiaohuruwei.error.log;
    # SSL certificate config. This uses a self-generated certificate, so browsers will warn about it; just choose to trust it.
    # For a publicly trusted certificate, you need to get one from a certificate authority
    ssl on;
    ssl_certificate /etc/nginx/ssl/getbase.crt;
    ssl_certificate_key /etc/nginx/ssl/getbase_nopass.key;
    location / {
        proxy_set_header Host $host;
        proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
        proxy_pass https://localhost:8443;
    }
}

Enabling HTTPS in GitLab

Having Nginx reverse-proxy HTTPS isn't enough on its own; you also need to turn on HTTPS support in GitLab.

Edit the configuration: add the following to gitlab.rb in /mnt/volumes/gitlab/config/:

# note the 'https' below
external_url "https://gitlab.example.com"

Create an ssl directory and put the SSL certificate files in it, named to match the domain above:

git.xiaohuruwei.com.crt
git.xiaohuruwei.com.key

Restart the container:

docker restart gitlab

Testing Access to GitLab

Open the web interface. The default login is root and the password is 5iveL!fe (since changed to the default password of Limi Jiaoyin, the company I was working for). Create a project repository: test.
Because the SSL certificate is self-generated and not trusted across the web, you have to choose to trust it for now. Set an environment variable locally:

export GIT_SSL_NO_VERIFY=1

Then clone the repository: git clone https://git.xiaohuruwei.com/root/test.git

Enabling Email

The default mail service doesn't work very well, so I configured my own. See the official GitLab SMTP documentation.

Using a 163.com mailbox and following the official docs, you'll find that emails don't get sent.

gitlab_rails['smtp_enable'] = true
gitlab_rails['smtp_address'] = "smtp.163.com"
gitlab_rails['smtp_port'] = 25
gitlab_rails['smtp_user_name'] = "xiaohuruwei@163.com"
gitlab_rails['smtp_password'] = "xxxx"
gitlab_rails['smtp_domain'] = "163.com"
gitlab_rails['smtp_authentication'] = "login"
gitlab_rails['smtp_enable_starttls_auto'] = true
gitlab_rails['smtp_tls'] = false
gitlab_rails['smtp_openssl_verify_mode'] = 'none'

The logs were messy and I didn't spot the problem in them. Later I found that someone in the Ruby community had solved the same problem:
GitLab 配置通过 smtp.163.com 发送邮件 (Sending GitLab email through smtp.163.com)
along with NetEase's official explanation:
NetEase's SMTP servers require the authentication account and the sender account to be the same; if they differ when a user sends an email, the email is rejected.

So I added two more lines, and after testing it worked:

gitlab_rails['gitlab_email_from'] = "xiaohuruwei@163.com"
user['git_user_email'] = "xiaohuruwei@163.com"

Access over SSH

Because GitLab is deployed with Docker, access over SSH (for example, git clone git@git.xiaohuruwei.com) goes through two layers of authentication:

One is authentication by the freelancer server.
The other is GitLab's own authentication.
The latter needs an SSH key.
The former might need a reverse proxy for SSH itself (the Nginx we use doesn't reverse-proxy anything other than HTTP and HTTPS).

For now, port forwarding turned out to be rather difficult, but you can change GitLab's default SSH port to a non-standard one by editing the variable directly in the GitLab configuration file:

gitlab_shell_ssh_port = 2222

Then restart the Docker container, and you'll see the SSH address change in the web interface:
ssh://git@git.xiaohuruwei.com:2222/root/test.git, after which you can carry on with git clone as usual.

Huilongguan, Beijing, January 2016

entry.title: Continuous Integration with DaoCloud: Deploying a Static Site and a Django App with Docker
entry.content:
A word before we start

From Wikipedia: Cargo cult programming

For readers who can't reach Wikipedia because the GFW (China's Great Firewall) blocks it:

Cargo cult programming is an anti-pattern in computer programming, characterized by the ritual use of code or program structures without understanding them. It is typically a sign that the programmer understands neither the bug they are trying to fix nor the apparent solution.

The term sometimes also refers to unskilled or inexperienced programmers copying code from one place to another without really knowing how it works, or whether it is needed in its new place. It can also mean applying design patterns, coding styles or programming methods incorrectly or excessively, without understanding the principles behind them.

Cargo cult programming takes its name from the term "cargo cult". A related coinage is "cargo cult software engineering".

When reading any tutorial, don't practice cargo cult programming. Some things need to be changed to fit your own situation, and you need to understand them. If you don't understand something, get familiar with the relevant background first.

About DaoCloud

DaoCloud offers a Docker-based continuous integration service. With it you can easily set up automated builds and continuous delivery for a project.

Of course, to use DaoCloud for continuous integration you first need to register a DaoCloud account. If you work for a company, you also need to ask the company to add your account to its user group, so that you can use the company's resources.

Continuous integration for a simple HTML5 app

Scenario for this section

  • You have your own host
  • You have added the host to DaoCloud
  • You only use DaoCloud's automated build and deployment features
  • The image is also deployed to your own host.

What is a "simple HTML5 app"

Front-end pages only, served by nginx.

The general approach to deployment

This post assumes one scenario: you have your own host, it is bound to DaoCloud, and you want to deploy continuously to that host through DaoCloud. To deploy a pure front-end project, you bundle nginx in and let nginx serve it.

Preparing before building the app

App directory structure

Because DaoCloud is based on Docker, before using DaoCloud we need to follow Docker's conventions and turn our project into an app that can be packaged into an image. For an HTML5 project, that means adding a Dockerfile and setting up the nginx config file it needs. For example, I have an app called jinli, with this directory structure (yours may well differ):

jinli/  # project root
├── jinli/  # the actual app directory
│   ├── images/ # images
│   ├── index.html  # default index html
│   ├── scripts/  #  js folder
│   └── styles/    # folder for css
├── Dockerfile   # Dockerfile
├── jinli.conf   # nginx config for this app
└── log/  # log files

In this structure, the file related to building the Docker image is the Dockerfile. jinli.conf is a file that will be packaged into the Docker image along with it. Everything else belongs to the app itself.

Creating the Dockerfile

A Dockerfile is Docker's rules file, much like a Makefile for make. It describes the process of building your app into a Docker image.
In this example, the Dockerfile looks like this:

# use the nginx service
FROM nginx:1.9.5
# copy the code
COPY . /src
# add the nginx config file
COPY jinli.conf /etc/nginx/conf.d/
# remove the default nginx config file
RUN rm /etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf

Explaining the Dockerfile:

  • First, picture the Docker image you're about to build as containing a Linux operating system.
  • FROM nginx:1.9.5 means: bring nginx version 1.9.5 into your image. (This is actually the step where the operating system comes in. nginx is itself an image built on top of a Linux operating system, so when you pull nginx, you pull it together with the whole Linux system it sits on.)
  • COPY . /src means: copy the code in the current directory to the /src directory in the image (in the image's operating system).
  • COPY jinli.conf /etc/nginx/conf.d/ means: copy the nginx config file you wrote in the current directory to the corresponding directory in the image (in its operating system).
  • Delete the original default nginx config (because the default config file takes up localhost; I don't know whether there is a better way around this).

Configuring the nginx config file used inside Docker

In this example, the nginx config file is named jinli.conf. It is packaged into the image to serve the HTML5 app. This is not very different from deploying directly on a server as usual. The things to watch are:

  • server_name is localhost, because this server_name is used inside the Docker container.
  • The root folder in location is a path inside the Docker container, not on the host machine.
server {
    listen 80;
    server_name localhost;
    access_log /src/log/jinli.access.log;
    error_log /src/log/jinli.error.log;
    # you can also add options such as gzip here as needed
    location / {
    root /src/jinli/;
    }
}

Then push the app to GitHub, for example to: xiaohuruwei/jinli.git

That's all the material you need. Now on to DaoCloud.

Using DaoCloud to build images and release continuously

The previous steps produced a Docker-ready version of the code, and it doesn't need to connect to external services like MySQL, so it can be built directly as a single-app image.

DaoCloud already has thorough documentation on this; you can follow its chapters on creating a new project and on continuous integration.

Section 4, Creating a new project: choose the git source to bind according to your situation
Section 5, Continuous integration and image building: for a simple HTML deployment, you don't need to know how to write daocloud.yml
Section 9: Releasing an app to your own host cluster

The core parts of the process above are:

  • Bind a git source
  • Choose the git repository to deploy and build it into an image
  • Deploy to your own host
  • Turn on the settings for subsequent automatic continuous deployment
  • In the "Settings" of the specific project under "Code Build", turn on continuous integration and set up the image and the CI trigger rules, for example: trigger automatic CI whenever code is pushed to the docker-support branch.
  • In the "Release" settings under "App List", turn on automatic release.

What to do after release

After release, you can see the details of the created container on DaoCloud, including the port mapped to the host. Click the port number to see the app's access address, and open it to test whether the deployment worked.

For convenience in what follows, assume the mapped port is 8888. Since we released to our own host, we also need to set up a domain and an nginx reverse proxy ourselves to serve external traffic. Assume a domain is already bound to the host; here, say, xiaohuruwei.com.

Log in to your host and configure nginx. If nginx was installed with a package manager like apt-get, add jinli.conf under /etc/nginx/conf.d/:

server {
    listen 80;
    server_name xiaohuruwei.com;
    access_log /var/log/nginx/jinli.access.log;
    error_log /var/log/nginx/jinli.error.log;
    client_max_body_size 200m;
    # you can set other options as needed
    location / {
        proxy_set_header Host $host;
        proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
        proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:8888;
    }
}

Then visit xiaohuruwei.com and you'll see the content.

Also, when using DaoCloud, turn on both automatic build and continuous release. That way, next time you only need to push code to GitHub; once your update rule is triggered, the image is rebuilt and released automatically.

Continuous integration for an app that depends on external services

Using a Django app as the example

Scenario this section applies to

  • You have your own host
  • You have added the host to DaoCloud
  • You only use DaoCloud's automated build and deployment features
    The external services it depends on already exist on your host (as Docker containers), and the image is also deployed to your own host. At deploy time, it connects to the external services already on the host (such as MySQL, Redis and so on).

Apps that depend on external services

In the Docker world, if a Docker image needs other images to provide services to it, we say the image has external services.

Take a simple Django app. If it can't do its job on its own and needs MySQL or another database for data persistence, then this Django app depends on external services.

Preparing before building

Preparation is close to the HTML5 case. Because it needs to connect to external services, and because uwsgi doesn't handle static files by default, there are a few more changes to the original code.

Project structure

First, the Django app's directory. Say there's an app called taikang, with this structure:

taikang    # project root    
├── Dockerfile    # Dockerfile
├── logs    
├── manage.py
├── Makefile    # makefile
├── requirements.txt    # python libraries the app depends on
├── templates
└── taikang        # app directory
    ├── __init__.py
    ├── models.py
    ├── settings.py   # django settings file
    ├── urls.py
    ├── views.py
    └── wsgi.py

Writing the Dockerfile
The Dockerfile means exactly the same thing as in the HTML5 deployment. Here it is:

# use python 2.7.10 as the base service
from python:2.7.10
copy everything in the current project into /src in the image
COPY . /src
# install the libraries the django app depends on, using the douban pypi mirror
RUN cd /src; pip install -r  requirements.txt -i http://pypi.douban.com/simple --trusted-host pypi.douban.com
# expose port 8000 from the image
EXPOSE 8000
# set the working directory to where the code is
WORKDIR  /src
# set the app's start command
CMD ["make", "start-uwsgi"]

Writing the Makefile

You may notice that the start command at the end uses make. That's what the Makefile in the directory structure above is for. I won't go into makefiles in detail here.
In short, it makes the app easier to manage. Here is the makefile:

# host and port uwsgi starts on
host:=0.0.0.0
port:=8000
# when debugging, start with django's built-in server
debug:
    ./manage.py runserver $(host):$(port)
# start the uwsgi service
start-uwsgi:
    uwsgi --socket $(host):$(port) \
        --chdir $(shell pwd) \
        --wsgi-file taikang/wsgi.py \
        --master \
        --process 4 \
        --pidfile $(shell pwd)/uwsgi.pid
# stop the uwsgi service
stop-uwsgi:
    uwsgi --stop uwsgi.pid
# reload the uwsgi service
reload-uwsgi:
    uwsgi --reload uwsgi.pid
# collect static files
collectstatic:
    ./manage.py collectstatic --noinput
.PHONY: debug \
    collectstatic \
    reload-uwsgi \
    start-uwsgi \
    stop-uwsgi

Static file support

When uwsgi serves the app, static files need to be handled separately. The currently recommended option is the whitenoise library for Django. It makes serving static files easy and needs only a few lines of configuration.

Connecting to services through environment variables

When deploying with Docker and you need to connect to external services, you usually do it through links plus environment variables. To support environment variables, our Django app needs some changes too: specifically, changing the configuration in settings.py.

Modify settings.py, using MySQL as the example:

# the original mysql config
#DATABASES = {
#    'default': {
#        'ENGINE': 'django.db.backends.mysql',
#        'NAME': 'starding_taikang',
#        'USER': 'root',
#        'PASSWORD': 'your_password_here',
#        'HOST': 'localhost',
#        'PORT': '3306'
#    }
#}
# get the service from environment variables
import os  # import the os library
mysql_name = os.environ.get('MYSQL_INSTANCE_NAME') or "taikang"  # get the database name
mysql_user = os.environ.get('MYSQL_USERNAME') or "root"  # get the mysql username
mysql_password = os.environ.get('MYSQL_PASSWORD') or "your_password"  # get the password
mysql_host = os.environ.get('MYSQL_ADDR') or "127.0.0.1"  # get the service address
mysql_port = "3306"
# use the variables above instead of strings
DATABASES = {
   'default': {
       'ENGINE': 'django.db.backends.mysql',
       'NAME': mysql_name,
       'USER': mysql_user,
       'PASSWORD': mysql_password,
       'HOST': mysql_host,
       'PORT': mysql_port
   }
}

Deploying the built taikang project with DaoCloud

The steps are basically the same as the HTML5 deployment. Suppose that after the image is built, its address is:

daocloud.io/xiaohuruwei/taking:latest

Next, when deploying from the image, you need to connect the external services, which means editing the yaml file by hand.

takang_test:
  image: daocloud.io/xiaohuruwei/taking:latest
  restart: always
  external_links:
  - mysql1:mysql      # mysql1 is the existing mysql container instance on your host; after the colon is the alias
  ports:
  - '8000'
  environment:    # environment variables    
  - MYSQL_ADDR=mysql

But this approach seems to have a bug. If it doesn't work, deploy directly first, and once that succeeds, edit the yaml file into the form above. When you edit the yaml file, DaoCloud will prompt you to redeploy; just confirm.

At this point the Django project is deployed too. Then, just like the HTML5 project, turn on automatic build and automatic release.

Note: because the Django project is deployed with uwsgi, visiting the address DaoCloud gives you directly won't work. You must configure an nginx reverse proxy.

Here is the nginx proxy config for a Django app deployed with uwsgi:

server {
    listen 80;
    server_name xiaohuruwei.com;
    access_log /var/log/nginx/taikang.access.log;
    error_log /var/log/nginx/taikang.error.log;
    client_max_body_size 200m;
    gzip on;
    gzip_min_length 1k;
    gzip_buffers 16 64k;
    gzip_http_version 1.1;
    gzip_comp_level 6;
    gzip_types text/plain application/x-javascript text/javascript text/css application/xml;
    gzip_vary on;
    location / {
        proxy_set_header Host $host;
        proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
        include uwsgi_params;
        uwsgi_pass 127.0.0.1:32801;
    }
}

Huilongguan, Beijing, January 2016

entry.title: Understanding Docker Through a Metaphor
entry.content:
The academic definition of Docker

Let's start with Wikipedia's definition:

Docker is an open-source project that automates the deployment of applications inside software containers, by providing an additional layer of abstraction and automation of operating-system-level virtualization on Linux. Docker uses the resource isolation features of the Linux kernel such as cgroups and kernel namespaces, and a union-capable filesystem such as aufs and others to allow independent “containers” to run within a single Linux instance, avoiding the overhead of starting and maintaining virtual machines.

From this fairly academic definition you can vaguely gather that Docker is a tool that automates things like deployment, but you can't really see what makes it so damn great, or where exactly its strengths lie. To figure that out, reading the definition is nowhere near enough. One way is to use Docker for a long time and gradually come to appreciate its advantages. But for a newcomer who has never touched Docker, and who may not even know much about deployment, how do you get there quickly? A good approach is to lean on a metaphor.

The Docker metaphor

The concept of "metaphor" gets its own post: "Metaphor"

Likewise, if you want to understand Docker quickly and grasp its core idea, a metaphor matters a lot.

The literal meaning: Docker, the dock worker

The name Docker is itself a metaphor. In the global logistics system, one of the most important inventions is the shipping container.

Why is the container so important? To see why, look at how logistics worked before containers existed: goods are produced and packed into crates, then loaded crate by crate onto a truck, then unloaded crate by crate and put on a train, carried to the station near the port, unloaded crate by crate again, loaded onto trucks, hauled to the freighter, loaded on crate by crate...

You can see that a huge amount of time, labor, and material goes to waste on all the loading and unloading in between. In logistics, the time goods actually spend on the road is fixed, and until transportation technology improves it's hard to shorten. So the time spent loading and unloading became the bottleneck of logistics, and that situation improved enormously once the container appeared.

What makes the container important is that it provides a universal, standard specification for packaging goods (put plainly, its size and shape conform to a standard). This produces a huge advantage: in transport, the goods only need to be packed once before shipping. The container can then go onto a train or a truck, be hauled to the port, be placed directly on the ship, and after unloading go straight onto a train or truck again to its destination. On top of that, the container's standard makes it very easy to handle mechanically, which kicked off a standardization of the entire global logistics system around the container. That saved enormous amounts of time and labor and accelerated the flow and reallocation of resources around the world.

Docker (the dock worker) borrows exactly the container metaphor

Docker is like the dock worker loading goods into a container: it packages your application into a container of a standard specification. In computing terms, this container packed to a given specification is called an "image." Really it's your original code plus some extra content, format, and so on, turned into a static application. And just as a disc image can only be parsed by software that understands that disc image format, this image can only be parsed by Docker.

The container reduces the work of transporting goods. What similar advantage does a Docker image offer? First, let's look at what deploying an application was like before Docker.

Before Docker, say I wanted to deploy a Django application. What would I have to do?
First I need a Python environment. Say I use Python 3 and your machine has Python 2. OK, install Python 3 first. Turns out that's a pain: you have to install all kinds of dependencies first and sort out possible conflicts. No way around it, so you grit your teeth and do it.

Once Python is installed, thanks to magical tools like pip, Django and the Python libraries you need go in quickly. Huh, turns out you also need MySQL, and Redis too. No way around it, keep going: download, install, configure. After a herculean effort it's finally done. And just like that, the day is gone.

What? You're telling me the old server is being retired and we're switching to a new one? Dammit, fine, let's do it all over again. With yesterday's experience, it only takes most of a day.

What? You're saying our app is so good we're going to promote it, and we need to walk other people through deploying it? I choose death. Delete the code and quit.

That description may be a bit exaggerated, but it's by no means rare. Before Docker, this is exactly what ops people spent much of their time doing, wasting huge amounts of manpower and resources on endlessly repeated work.

After Docker

A standard deliverable

Saying Docker is like a shipping container, the key point is "standardization." What is its concrete product? It's the "image." Honestly, the Chinese word for it, jingxiang (镜像, "mirror image"), sounds pretty mystical, and the original English word "image" is pretty mystical too. It's mystical because its original meaning has been extended for special contexts. It originally means "picture, likeness," and a picture also carries the sense of "an abstract depiction of a real object." A picture can also be copied easily, which later gave it the sense of "a copy of the original picture," and later still it was used directly for disc images (something that stores an image and is easy to copy, except that a picture is drawn on paper while this kind of image exists digitally on a disc). Of course, jingxiang already means "copy" in Chinese, but it picks up the particular mood of Chinese characters and comes across as mystical and hazy.

"Image" was later extended further. In Docker, it means taking your application itself and packaging it in a certain format (really just a series of command lines executed according to rules) into something with a standard specification (much like a container packaging your goods). It's just like how a disc image packages the original content into a format that can be burned directly onto a disc. This format can only be parsed by Docker itself, just as your disc image can only be parsed by specific tools.

In Docker, an image can't be run directly. My guess is that this isn't for technical reasons but for engineering-design reasons. Generally, a specific version of a piece of software gets packaged into exactly one image. If an image could be configured and run, it could easily get damaged in use.

So how do you avoid that? Add another layer, which amounts to a cloning technique: as long as the original body is fine, the clones can crash and burn all they like without anything really dying. This extra clone layer is called a container. The name is pretty apt: it's like a bottle or some other vessel, your application runs inside it, and you get an extra layer of safety. If you want to use a service or get your application running, you just create a new container from the image (also a single command), while the image itself stays put, untouched. Can't help it, it's precious.

Roughly speaking, there are two kinds of images:

One kind, let's simply call base standalone images. Each is usually a standalone service, and the most standalone service images of all are the various stripped-down operating systems. They're packaged into images as the most basic service, and practically every image depends on one. But for ordinary application developers like us, we generally don't use these images directly.
If we do use one, our Dockerfile usually looks something like this:

# Base operating system
From ubuntu:latest
# Build the other services we need, plus our own code
RUN apt-get install mysql
COPY .  /src/

The other kind, let's call composite images. They're built on top of a standalone image, combining other services on top of it, such as a Python service or something like MySQL. As fairly top-level application developers, we generally use these pre-combined service images directly.
The Dockerfile then looks something like this:

# Base python service
From python:2.7.10 
# Our own code
RUN apt-get install mysql
COPY .  /src/

In fact, a Python service like the one above is itself built on top of a base operating system. If you look at the Python Dockerfile on Docker Hub, this becomes clear:

FROM buildpack-deps:jessie    # jessie is a stripped-down debian operating system
# remove several traces of debian python
RUN apt-get purge -y python.*

The images we build ourselves can also be called a kind of composite image. We usually use a Dockerfile to combine our own application code with some of the specific service images above (such as python), and that's how we build our own application.

What exactly does Docker simplify?

Docker takes exactly those repetitive parts of the deployment process and does them automatically. You only need to build a working Docker image during the first deployment. After that, a few short commands are enough to pull the image, create a container from it, and get the service running. All you need is a server with Docker installed, a Dockerfile, and a reasonably smooth network connection. Truly "build once, deploy anywhere."

Need a Python 3 environment? Just from python:3.x and you're done.
Need to migrate servers? Copy the application along with its Dockerfile and volumes data to the new server, a few commands, done again.
Need to offer it as a service to others? The Dockerfile is the clearest deployment document there is. Maintain an official image, and whoever needs it just pulls it down and deploys it with a few commands.
By now you may have noticed that the Docker image has become a standard shipping unit, just like a container. Unlike traditional software delivery, which just hands you the code and some documentation and calls it a day, it hands you a standard Docker shipment directly. That might be a Dockerfile, or the image itself, and this standard unit includes not only the code but the whole environment the code runs in, including the OS.

So whoever wants to use my service just pulls the image and instantiates a container, and it directly provides the service you need. No more tedious installation process like before: someone has already done all of that for you.

And the advantages don't stop there

Just as the "standardization" the container brought to logistics didn't only affect the container itself, but standardized and improved the efficiency of the whole field, from transport machinery to logistics management.

In other words, once you have "standardization" of one core thing, you can do much more on top of it, like automated mechanical handling of containers. Docker is similar: once this kind of standard software unit is established, the standard unit and the corresponding ways of managing it can bring about many more changes. For example:

Unified service management

Applications deployed with Docker all fall within Docker's management. This is another huge advantage of Docker: it provides an isolated space and brings the scattered applications deployed on a server together under centralized management.

For example, say I have a ton of services deployed on one server: MySQL, Redis, RabbitMQ, plus a pile of other applications. One day the server suddenly loses power and reboots. Brace yourself for a tragedy. The apps that weren't set to restart automatically, the apps that broke on restart, the important apps hiding in some corner you didn't even know about that failed to start...

With Docker, though, you can see at a glance which applications started normally and which ones have problems. Then you just deal with them methodically, and you're fine.

Use in continuous delivery

Continuous delivery is somewhat beyond the scope here. Go find the answers yourself.

A misconception about Docker

Someone might ask: I only have one server, and I'm unlikely to migrate. My Python service and MySQL service only need to be deployed once and can be reused from then on. Does Docker still have any advantage for me? After all, Docker has a learning cost too.

If you're really sure your applications are one-off and only for your own use, then Docker's advantage in this scenario isn't especially obvious: even with Docker, someone has to do the initial build, and that's work. It's about the same amount of work as a one-time deployment. Even so, it still has an upside: it gives you a clean, isolated environment.

Also, when many people say Docker changed the world of ops, they're speaking at the level of the whole community. For applications with huge user bases like MySQL and Python, and for applications that are frequently migrated, changed, and redeployed, the time saved across the whole community after Dockerizing them is enormous.

That is, Docker can't reduce deployment work "to zero." In the good case it's "reduced to basically one," because no matter what, you have to build the application and its environment once. Just as the container eliminates the handling along the way but can't avoid the one operation of loading the goods into the container. But that one build can become the foundation of "build once, deliver anywhere." The first time you build your own image is similar to loading a container: it takes about as much work as deploying directly on the machine. At that point, Docker's efficiency gain is very small.

But are you really sure the work you're doing is only a one-off?

Huilongguan, Beijing, January 2016

entry.title: Closures and Decorators in Python
entry.content:
First version created: 2016-01-06

Closures

Let's start with the definition from Wikipedia:

In programming languages, closures (also lexical closures or function closures) are a technique for implementing lexically scoped name binding in languages with first-class functions. Operationally, a closure is a record storing a function together with an environment: a mapping associating each free variable of the function (variables that are used locally, but defined in an enclosing scope) with the value or storage location to which the name was bound when the closure was created. A closure—unlike a plain function—allows the function to access those captured variables through the closure’s reference to them, even when the function is invoked outside their scope

Then let's examine the definition:

There are a few key points in the passage above:

  • A closure is a technique.
  • A closure is a record made up of a function and the environment it lives in.
  • When a closure, i.e. the record above, is created, it binds the free variables used in the function (variables defined in an enclosing lexical scope but used locally in the function) to their values.
  • Unlike a plain function, a closure lets the function use the variables it has captured (bound), even when those variables are defined outside its scope.
    Looking only at the definition, plus whatever intuition the word "closure" gives you, you end up with a fuzzy idea at best: this thing is roughly some enclosed structure that contains a function and variables defined outside the function. To understand it more deeply, you have to look at real code.

An example of a closure in Python:

# function that creates the closure
def counter(start_at=0):
    count = [start_at]
    def incr():
        count[0] += 1
        return count[0]
    return incr
# assign the closure to another variable
counter1 = counter()
# assign it to yet another variable
counter2 = counter(5)

In the code above, counter is a function that creates closures, and the next two lines assign its results to two different variables. This actually produces two closures, counter1 and counter2, each consisting of the function itself plus a scope attached to it from outside the function.

These two closures are a lot like two instantiated objects: the scopes attached to them outside the function are independent and don't affect each other.

Decorators

First, the literal meaning.
The word "decorator" literally means "a tool for decorating some particular thing." Implicit in the word is the idea that the thing being decorated is the core, while the decorating tool is just an embellishment that adds a little something extra.

Take a metaphor: at Christmas we hang little ornaments on the Christmas tree. Each ornament is a small decorator, and the core being decorated is the tree. This also implies that the tree is what matters; the ornaments merely give it some extra fun features.

It's similar in Python. Python doesn't actually have an object type called "decorator" the way it has functions, dicts and lists. Rather, Python lets you build a certain kind of callable (usually a function or a class) that can be used to decorate other objects, and we call any object with this decorating ability a decorator. At bottom, it's just a callable that plays a decorating role.

That raises two questions:

What does it decorate?
And how does it do the decorating?
Again, let's look at code. An example of a Python decorator:

import time
from functools import wraps
# the main function being decorated
def foo():
    # do whatever we actually want to do
    # ...
    # ...
    # and finally print something
    print 'in foo()'
# the decorator    
def timeit(func):
    '''
    Decorator that reports the execution time.
   '''
   @wraps(func)
    def wrapper(*args, **kwargs):
        start  = time.clock()
        result = func(*args, **kwargs)
        end = time.clock()
        print 'used: {0}'.format(end-start)
        return result
    return wrapper

First we need to be clear about what the core of our program is. We want the foo function to carry out some specific task and print something at the end, so our core function is foo.

At the same time, we'd also like to know how long the task takes, which is exactly something a decorator can do. So we build a function, timeit, as a decorator to decorate foo.

One point worth stressing again: the decorator timeit exists to decorate foo. It only adds the ability to report execution time; it doesn't change what foo was meant to do. It has no effect whatsoever on foo's original job.

If you look closely, though, you'll notice that the decorator above uses closures (just not very visibly, since it doesn't carry an extra scope along, though adding one would be fine). More precisely, both closures and decorators rest on the fact that callables in Python can be passed around.

The Decorator Pattern

So where do decorators come from? The idea comes from the decorator pattern in design patterns: without changing the core object being called, add some interesting and possibly useful features to it. That is exactly what "decorating" means.

You don't have to touch the original core object at all, and you still get what you want. Pretty clever.

Huilongguan, Beijing, January 2016

entry.title: Origins
entry.content:
Come to think of it, I've been blogging for quite a while

Looking back over these years, I started trying to blog in my first year of college. Back then I didn't know much about technology, so most of my posts were miscellaneous essays, mostly my thoughts on current events.

At first I didn't even know independent blogs existed, and I posted everything on QQ Zone (a social blogging space attached to the QQ messenger). That was because QQ Zone was the only place I knew of where you could publish and keep journal entries online, so I used it as a blog. QQ Zone did have some advantages: since it was built on the QQ social platform, whatever I wrote could always be seen by friends and others, and I'd get some feedback now and then, which was one of the things that kept me writing.

But later, as what I wrote leaned more and more toward my major, and I rarely wrote those essays that oozed edgy teenage thinking anymore, QQ Zone's advantages faded. Its writing experience was also terrible (laggy, rich text only): fine for a short plain-text post, hopeless once a post had a few more elements.

I've blogged in a lot of places

So I went looking for other places to blog: Douban, NetEase and so on. But they were either awful to write in or full of ads that really spoiled the mood. Around then I happened to learn about independent blogs. So I registered a domain, bought a server, set up my own WordPress, hunted for a good theme, and after a lot of tinkering finally had my own independent blog.

After having it for a little over a year, though, I found that I spent less time on the writing itself than on maintaining the blog. One headache after another, until I was too worn out to care anymore.

That's when I realized writing was the real goal all along, and I no longer wanted to spend effort maintaining an independent blog. So began my second search for a suitable writing platform. I tried a wave of them, NetEase's Lofter among others, and only Jianshu was more or less acceptable, but Jianshu wasn't very customizable.

Then it also hit me that I'd used far too many platforms, and what I'd written was scattered all over the place, which was bad for building up and organizing my own knowledge. So I decided to keep looking.

In the end I found GitHub's twin: GitHub Pages.

Bringing it all together at last

GitHub is where programmers hang out most anyway, and GitHub Pages had great reviews. It took me just half a day to set up a semi-independent blog, and one look at the result told me this was exactly what I wanted.

And so began the road to bringing it all together...

Later I happened to see someone online summarize "the three stages of blogging," and it rang very true. Here it is:

Stage one: you've just discovered blogging, it feels fresh, and you try writing on some free hosting service.

Stage two: you find the free service too restrictive, so you buy your own domain and hosting and set up an independent blog.

Stage three: you find managing an independent blog too much hassle, and ideally you'd keep control while someone else handles the management, so you only have to write.

.
.
.
.
.

An addendum from February 2024

Reopening My Independent Blog
